Article Title: 'This is real': Pete Hegseth appears to mock Canadian military woman amid US-Canada tensions
Article Text:
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth appeared to take a weight-related jab at a uniformed woman pictured in a Canadian cadet. (Photo: ANI)

Hegseth has repeatedly used ‘fit not fat’

Trade talks collapse, tariffs rise

Canada targets more than 700 US products

Trump rhetoric raises sovereignty tensions

US secretary of war Pete Hegseth appeared to mock the appearance of a uniformed woman featured in a Canadian cadet post on Tuesday, sharing her image on X with a Canadian flag and the words: “(this is real)”.The image, originally posted by the cadets.vernon Instagram account, showed the woman in Canadian military camouflage standing alongside another person in cadet attire. Hegseth did not explain what he meant or make any explicit reference to her weight. However, the post was widely interpreted as a weight-related jibe given his repeated use of the phrase “fit not fat” while pushing tougher physical standards in the US military.Canada’s Cadet Instructors Cadre is part of the Canadian Armed Forces Reserve. It comprises approximately 7,800 commissioned officers whose primary responsibility is the safety, supervision, administration and training of more than 52,000 cadets, according to Canada’s Department of National Defence.Weight and physical fitness have been recurring themes in Hegseth’s push for tougher standards in the US military.At the US Army War College in April 2025, he told military leaders they needed to be “fit not fat, sharp not shabby” while discussing a force-wide review of fitness, training and physical standards.His language became more pointed at a gathering of senior US military commanders at Quantico in September 2025.“It’s completely unacceptable to see fat generals and admirals in the halls of the Pentagon,” Hegseth said while laying out stricter fitness and appearance standards. In the same speech, he also complained about seeing “fat troops” in military formations. The Pentagon subsequently issued new guidance on physical fitness and grooming standards.The language continued into 2026. In February, Hegseth praised the US Army on X by writing: “Well done @USArmy. Merit-based & Fit NOT Fat.”At West Point in May, he told graduating cadets: “You're fit, not fat. You are disciplined, not distracted.”Hegseth’s post about the Canadian cadet programme also comes at a particularly sensitive moment in relations between Washington and Ottawa, with the two neighbours locked in an escalating trade dispute and tensions rising over Canadian sovereignty.Trade negotiations broke down in late August after Canada rejected last-minute US terms and suspended the talks. The United States subsequently imposed 50% tariffs on C$27.6 billion worth of Canadian goods.The Trump administration has accused Canadian policies of discriminating against US businesses, including in sectors such as motor vehicles and dairy, and imposed the duties under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930.Canada disputes Washington’s case. Prime Minister Mark Carney said last-minute changes to the US proposal were “unfair, uneconomic” and called into question the reliability of any agreement. He said Ottawa would not accept terms that undermined Canadian interests and sovereignty.Among the sticking points were automobiles and broader questions over Canada’s ability to make independent decisions on trade and domestic policy.From September 8, Canada will impose retaliatory tariffs of 15%, 25% and 50% on C$27.6 billion worth of US imports.The measures cover hundreds of American products and include sectors such as steel, dairy, household appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics. Ottawa says the countermeasures will match the US tariffs dollar for dollar.The stakes are considerable. The United States and Canada traded nearly $880 billion worth of goods and services in 2025, while about 72% of Canadian goods exports went to the US.The two economies are particularly closely integrated in sectors such as automobiles, where vehicles and components routinely move across the border during the manufacturing process.Carney has also pushed to reduce Canada’s dependence on the US market by expanding trade relationships elsewhere.Trade is only one source of friction. Trump has repeatedly suggested that Canada could become the 51st US state, remarks rejected by Canadian leaders and which have added a sovereignty dimension to the economic confrontation.The rhetoric took another turn on August 27, when Trump signed an executive order directing the US government to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”.The order directs the US interior secretary and Board on Geographic Names to update federal references to the lake. The change applies to US federal usage and does not determine what Canada or international bodies call it.Canada’s retaliatory tariffs are due to take effect on September 8, with trade negotiations between the two countries still suspended.
Article Summary: US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth appeared to mock the appearance of a uniformed woman featured in a Canadian cadet post. The image, originally posted by the cadets.vernon Instagram account, showed the woman in Canadian military camouflage standing alongside another person in cadet attire. The post was widely interpreted as a weight-related jibe given his repeated use of the phrase “fit not fat” while pushing tougher physical standards in the US military.

Article Title: What happens when a historic celebrity home is demolished? Richard Gere’s $10.75 million Connecticut estate is gone, but where did the 1938 oak library, marble fireplace, antique doorway and other pie
Article Text:
Pic credit: Realtor.com

The former celebrity owners

Pic credit: Realtor.com

What got saved

Pic credit: Realtor.com

Richard Gere’s former New Canaan, Connecticut, home sat empty for less than a year before being demolished last year. In October 2024, Richard Gere, 75, and his wife, Alejandra Gere, 42, sold their New Canaan, Conn. , property for $10.75 million before relocating to Spain. By August 2025, the 1938 historic brick Georgian Colonial-style country manor was gone. The manor was reduced to an empty parcel of land, and the new owners plan to divide the plot into nine lots that could fit as many luxury homes.And just like that, the 87-year-old historic home was gone. The wrecking ball swept through what was once a six-bedroom house complete with a koi pond, a courtyard and enough architectural detail to make preservationists wince! So, before the trucks arrived, the salvage team sprang into action to rescue what could be saved. "We recently checked in, and the house has been taken down. We are grateful that the buyers allowed us time to salvage and get everything out,” salvage company owner Reggie Young told People.It’s been a year since the house was demolished. But what happened to the cerused oak library, Italian marble mantels and hand-carved stone doorways?The historic manor has seen many elite owners ever since it was built in 1938. Richard Gere and his wife purchased the Connecticut estate from legendary singer Paul Simon in 2022 for $10.8 million, a discount from its listing price.Simon and his wife, Edie Brickell, bought the property in 2002 for a whopping $16.5 million. The couple had owned it longer, watching their daughter Lulu grow up in its rooms. When Gere sold it two years later, he triggered a chain reaction that would ultimately undo nearly a century of history. No wonder Lulu reacted the way she did. In a since-deleted Instagram post, Lulu conveyed that she was not happy with the demolition. “Just in case anyone was wondering if I still hate Richard Gere—I do!" And she has her reasons for that.Gere sold it to the developer, SBP Homes, and they transformed the 32-acre lot into a nine-property luxury subdivision, turning it into the largest new residential project New Canaan has seen since 2007. The plot was turned into a nine-lot subdivision ranging in size from 2.2 to 4.8 acres, according to CT Insider. The plan was to sell the land in parcels, empty. They knew wealthy buyers would buy it and build their own vision. "We’re very excited about this project. From the beginning, our goal was to thoughtfully accommodate a wide range of interests in how the property would be developed," SBP Homes project manager Adam Sherer said in a statement.And just like any other developer project, there is rarely room for sentiment or preservation. So, no, the developer had no sentiment for Lulu’s childhood home, even though it was historic. The cost of maintaining a 1938 Colonial while carving a subdivision around it didn't pencil out. The legal complications of heritage designation were even more complicated. So demolition was the only way forward for the developers.In May 2025, a New York salvage company called Hudson Valley House Parts was called in to salvage parts of the 1938 six-bedroom brick Colonial, according to Realtor.com. "It's so important that the developers allowed the project to be salvaged," Young told People. He added that it was ‘a real shame’ that the house was being torn down. "Once the stuff is gone, it's never coming back,” he told Realtor.com.The firm managed to rescue various unique elements from the property, including an oak library, nautical-themed bay windows, limestone and marble mantels and other architectural features. They were too good to be torn out in the demolition.All these were priceless in the market, as high-end homebuyers often seek to add historical character to new spaces. So there is a demand for marble mantels, refurbished wood flooring and antique hardware. However, there's a gap between demand and actual execution. Most of these demolished homes never get properly salvaged; as a result, only 20 to 30 per cent of construction and demolition debris is recovered for reuse, according to the Environmental Protection Agency.However, Gere’s house had better luck. The octagonal bluestone patio, complete with what Hudson Valley House Parts described as ‘exceptional patina’, was lifted and palletised. The colonial window sashes went into storage. A limestone mantel travelled to a buyer in New Orleans. The ornate doorway with fanned glass and Egyptian columns found a new home in a Colonial Revival renovation in Indiana."Mantels are popular," Young said. He added that "a good marble mantel usually goes for $4,000 to $8,000."Other parts of the home that were salvaged include the nautical motifs made of steel, the mid-century bay windows, a limestone mantel and a marble mantel; a complete cerused oak library with a curved fireplace and built-in wall panelling; exterior stone steps with an iron railing; a portico; and the entire entryway with its arched jamb, door surround and panelled walls. The bluestone edge of the koi pond was also rescued.The oak library panels, the stone patio and the marble mantel may find another house. But the 1938 house itself, the one with 87 years of history, is erased, and the land now awaits a new one.
Article Summary: Richard Gere and his wife, Alejandra Gere, sold their New Canaan, Connecticut, property for $10.75 million in October 2024. In May 2025, a New York salvage company called Hudson Valley House Parts was called in to salvage parts of the 1938 six-bedroom brick Colonial. The firm managed to rescue various unique elements from the property, including an oak library, nautical-themed bay windows, limestone and marble mantels.

Article Title: Australian high school students collected more than 2,000 plastic bottles to form a greenhouse, 11 years later, the structure supplies food for the school's garden
Article Text:
The construction combines hands-on learning with materials that would otherwise have ended up in a landfill.

A project that began as an ecological lesson has transformed the lives of students at an Australian high school. In the country's capital of Canberra, students at the Richardson Primary School in south Canberra collected more than 2,000 plastic bottles and transformed them into the walls of a greenhouse that has been working efficiently for the past decade, as reported by ABC News. The project called Plastic Palace, was inaugurated on June 24, 2015, with a grant of AU$2,000 from the Teachers Mutual Bank Environment Fund. Eleven years later, the structure is still standing and provides food for the school's garden.The idea originated in 2012 with Kate Davis, a sixth-grade teacher at the school, who proposed to her students that they transform everyday waste into an educational resource. The bottle collection lasted for a year and a half, with participation from students, teachers and families from across the school. "At first, we thought 2,000 bottles would be enough, but the original plan grew in scale," explained Davis, who led the project from her classroom.In order to build the walls of the greenhouse, the bottles were cleaned and strung on columns attached to a wooden frame, mounted on the original earthen floor of the patio. Their translucent bodies allow light to pass through and protect the plants inside from the wind while the bottoms of the bottles are reused as pots for seedlings that are later transplanted to the garden.The construction combines hands-on learning with materials that would otherwise have ended up in a landfill.The grant given by the fund covered the cost of timber, tools and seeds and helped complete the construction. The greenhouse was officially opened on June 24, 2015, with the then Minister of Education for the Australian Capital Territory, Joy Burch, in attendance. "It's a fantastic example of reduce, reuse, and recycle," Burch said at the opening.The school's headteacher, Jason Borton, recalled how the students worked with their teacher until the greenhouse dream became a reality. What began as a one-class project ended up involving the entire school, and today the Plastic Palace remains an integral part of science classes, the school garden, and the chickens. The seedlings that sprout among the bottles are eventually transplanted into the outdoor garden beds."It has also helped them realise that something you use every day can be transformed into something else," summarised Kate Davis, the teacher who spearheaded the project from the year it was first proposed.Moreover, when it comes to nurturing the greenhouse plants, the vegetable patch and tending to the school's chooks, the students are in charge. "Really, they do everything in the garden. The classes come out to plant and they cultivate the food," said Borton. "The greenhouse is the breeding ground for the seedlings, then the students transfer them to the garden so they can see how food gets to the table."
Article Summary: Students at the Richardson Primary School in south Canberra collected more than 2,000 plastic bottles and transformed them into the walls of a greenhouse. The project called Plastic Palace, was inaugurated on June 24, 2015, with a grant of AU$2,000 from the Teachers Mutual Bank Environment Fund. Eleven years later, the structure is still standing and provides food for the school's garden.

Article Title: A YouTuber spent 4 years helping strangers find lost relatives; then a DNA test gave him a 22.7% match with a 66-year-old Texas woman who turned out to be his long-lost sister
Article Text:
Blair Clark and his wife Leah and details of DNA testing kit from MyHeritage.

A family divided by social stigma

66 years waiting for answers

From helping others to finding his own family

Blair Clark and his wife Leah have spent more than four years on their YouTube show, The Leah and Blair Slog, helping people reconnect with relatives they’ve never known, or lost touch with. The couple, who live in the Philippines, have helped adoptees find biological parents and Amerasian Filipinos find fathers once stationed at U.S. naval and air bases. But in a remarkable twist Blair has recently become the seeker of a missing part of his own family history. According to a report by Upworthy, Blair was given a DNA testing kit from MyHeritage, a family history and genetic testing company. He signed up for the platform and found a 22.7% DNA match with a 66-year-old woman in San Antonio, Texas, named Fiona. The match suggested Fiona could be an aunt or a half-sister. As Blair started to look into the connection, the evidence was pointing more and more to an incredible conclusion: Fiona was his long-lost sister. The find was especially poignant as Blair had known a family secret since the age of 20. His mother, Isabel, told him that she'd had a child when she was 19, and she'd placed the baby for adoption.Isabel’s story was a painful truth faced by many unmarried mothers in the United Kingdom after the Second World War, states the news report.Women who had children out of wedlock were often stigmatized and in many cases pressured to give their children up for adoption. It also reports that around 200,000 mothers were forced to give children up for adoption in the 30 years after the war, during the UK's war-time generation. Isabel died aged 59 in 1999, never finding out that her daughter would be identified decades later. And then, Fiona was adopted shortly after birth and brought up in Scotland and Bermuda. Over the years she has worked in the oil industry, human resources and retail management. Ultimately, her life took her to Louisiana, Yemen and San Antonio, Texas. She later had two daughters, three grandsons and a great-grandson.Fiona opened a MyHeritage account about 10 years ago, leaving the door open for a family find. The long-awaited connection finally appeared after Blair joined the platform. The two then met over Zoom, where Fiona found out Blair was her brother, and she had three brothers in all. One of the most moving moments was when Fiona was shown a picture of Isabel. She'd never known her mother, but seeing her face suddenly gave a tangible connection to the woman whose identity had been a mystery all her life. Fiona’s similarity to their mother made the discovery all the more powerful for Blair. The picture helped cement his understanding that the woman he had known only in family lore for years had left behind another daughter.There was a strange irony in Blair’s discovery. For years he and Leah had sat behind the camera, helping strangers find family histories and witness emotional reunions. Suddenly, Blair was experiencing the same uncertainty, excitement and sense of closure as the people he had previously helped. The experience also gave him a greater appreciation of what those reunions meant to those involved, especially Fiona, who lived 65 years without knowing her biological identity or family. Now the newly discovered siblings are working to build the relationship they never had growing up. Blair lives in the Philippines and two of his brothers are in Australia. The four siblings hope to meet up in Thailand around the end of 2026, starting a new chapter for a family separated for more than six decades. A GoFundMe campaign is underway to help fund the reunion. Separated for a lifetime, the siblings now have a chance not only to learn of their common past but to build a future together, concludes the news report by Upworthy.Images Courtesy: Facebook and Upworthy
Article Summary: Blair Clark and his wife Leah have spent more than four years on their YouTube show, The Leah and Blair Slog, helping people reconnect with relatives they’ve never known. Blair was given a DNA testing kit from MyHeritage, a family history and genetic testing company. He signed up for the platform and found a 22.7% DNA match with a 66-year-old woman in San Antonio, Texas, named Fiona. The two then met over Zoom, where Fiona found out Blair was her brother, and she had three brothers in all.

Article Title: Meet Aditi Paudel, a 17-year-old high school student appointed as Japan's first literacy ambassador
Article Text: Born in Japan, and raised in Nepal during her early childhood, Aditi Paudel had always shown an affinity towards reading. Her earliest memory of reading is of her grandfather handing her a newspaper filled with intricate Devanagari script when she was still in preschool. But to the surprise of those around her, she was still able to make sense of the text. Over the years, she has only improved and the now 17-year-old high school senior in Tokyo was recently appointed as Japan's first literacy ambassador, as per a report by The Japan Times.The World Literacy Foundation, a global nonprofit headquartered in Australia is running a program where around 900 young people between the ages of 16 and 25 from 101 countries are participating. While the program has been running for 12 years, this is the first time an ambassador from Japan has been appointed, according to Andrew Kay, CEO and founder of the World Literacy Foundation.The aim of the program is to connect young people around the world and get them “involved and waving the flag for literacy in their community,” Kay said, noting that Paudel was singled out “for her leadership, passion for literacy, and commitment to empowering young people in Japan.”“Her curiosity about English shaped thoughtful advocacy, strengthening the program’s global voice and cultural reach,” he added.Paudel returned to Japan to enter the third grade and along with settling into a new life, she found herself having to learn Japanese once more, which meant turning to the books. Her love for reading came pretty early in her life, nurtured by her father who bought her plenty of books. She developed an early taste for fantasy, and recalled falling in love with Enid Blyton’s “The Wishing-Chair.”Reading Malala Yousafzai 's autobiography, 'I Am Malala', helped her develop significant interests in female empowerment, including ensuring that women across the world have access to education and literacy. Along with working with children with disabilities, she plans to work with the Shanti Volunteer Association to collect and donate books to Asian countries with lower rates of literacy, including Nepal.With enough experience developing her own reading skills, Paudel said that a common view of literacy is how well a person can read or write, but she sees it in broader terms. Essentially, it’s “something that helps you open doors for more opportunities,” she noted.Paudel has experienced the impact of her access to private education firsthand and how it has set her life on a different course. “My parents grew up in a completely opposite environment. They did not have a childhood like this,” she said. “Being literate is so important because even though you have the potential, you can never unlock it if you do not have literacy.”But even those with easy access to books are reading less than they once did. Around half of elementary, junior high and high school age children in Japan do not read books, according to a recent study by Benesse Educational Research & Development Institute and the University of Tokyo.Fewer young people are reading for pleasure and enjoyment, said Kay, and that could cause a significant regressive effect. “As far as embedding themselves in a novel or reading something that really takes a little bit more effort, that is becoming a rarer thing,” he said. Kay also cautions against the impact of artificial intelligence, noting that the latest tech tools provide quick answers, allowing people to skip the process of researching, reading and wrestling with theories and thoughts oneself.“It’s turning our clock back 150 years … where most people couldn’t read or would have limited ability to read,” he said of the absence of reading books as a mainstream pursuit. Those trends only add importance to initiatives like the World Literacy Foundation’s ambassador program.As a teenager, Paudel understands growing up in a world full of distractions, where much of life is on and from social media. “You will always be more inclined to go for your phone rather than a book,” she said, and because of this, making reading a habit is critical. Her advice for developing a love of reading isn’t about ticking classics off a book list, but finding something that resonates, and that, ideally, can broaden the reader’s perspective.
Article Summary: Aditi Paudel, a 17-year-old high school senior in Tokyo, was recently appointed as Japan's first literacy ambassador. The World Literacy Foundation, a global nonprofit headquartered in Australia is running a program where around 900 young people between the ages of 16 and 25 from 101 countries are participating.

Article Title: Melinda French Gates' father worked on NASA's Apollo missions; the women engineers she met at his company picnics shaped her thinking
Article Text:
Melinda French Gates' father worked on NASA's Apollo missions

The women engineers she met became important examples

Company picnics offered her a different view of women's careers

Her parents made education a priority

She eventually chose computer science

Apollo showed her what science could accomplish

Her mother's influence reinforced the importance of opportunity

From technology to a wider mission for women

Why seeing women in science mattered

The childhood lesson that followed her into adulthood

Melinda French Gates grew up in a household where science, engineering and education were closely woven into family life. Her father, Raymond Joseph French Jr., was an aerospace engineer whose career included work connected to NASA's Apollo programme, giving his daughter an early glimpse into the world of space exploration and advanced technology. But some of the most influential experiences from her childhood happened away from laboratories and launch sites. At company picnics connected to her father's workplace, French Gates met women who worked as engineers and mathematicians, seeing first-hand that women could build careers in technical fields. Those encounters helped shape her understanding of what was possible for women and girls, an idea that would later become a recurring theme in her own career, technology work and philanthropic efforts.Raymond French's career in aerospace placed him close to one of the most ambitious technological projects of the 20th century. He worked for the aerospace industry during the era of the Apollo programme, America's effort to send astronauts to the Moon and return them safely to Earth. For French Gates, this meant the space programme was not simply something she watched on television. Her father's work gave the family a personal connection to the engineering effort behind the missions.She has spoken about growing up in Dallas and watching Apollo launches with her family, while understanding that her father was involved in the broader aerospace world that made such missions possible. The experience exposed her from an early age to the idea that mathematics, science and engineering could be used to solve extraordinarily difficult problems.The people French Gates encountered through her father's professional life were arguably just as influential as the technology surrounding the Apollo era. She has recalled meeting women who worked in technical positions at company picnics and other gatherings associated with her father's workplace. Her father talked about women mathematicians working on his teams and made sure his daughters could see these women as real professionals. For a young girl growing up during a period when engineering and technology were still overwhelmingly associated with men, that visibility mattered. The women were not presented as an abstract argument about equality. They were people she could meet, speak with and observe pursuing demanding careers. Seeing them helped demonstrate that technical ability and professional ambition were not limited by gender.A company picnic might seem like an ordinary family event, but for French Gates it provided an unusual form of career exposure. She could see women participating in the same professional world as her father and contributing to complex technical work. That experience mattered because children often form ideas about what careers are available to them from the people they see around them. A girl who rarely encounters women in engineering may unconsciously conclude that the field is not meant for her. French Gates instead encountered women who challenged that assumption. The lesson was subtle but powerful. Women could be mathematicians, engineers and technology professionals, and they could contribute meaningfully to some of the most challenging projects of their time.Her father's career was only one part of the environment that encouraged French Gates to pursue education. Her mother, Elaine French, also placed enormous importance on giving her children opportunities that she herself had not received. French Gates grew up as one of four children, and her parents expected all of them to attend university. The family worked to make higher education financially possible, reinforcing the idea that education was an investment rather than a luxury. This emphasis eventually helped lead French Gates to Duke University, where she studied computer science and economics before earning an MBA. The combination of her father's technical background and her parents' belief in education created an environment in which pursuing a demanding academic path was encouraged rather than discouraged.French Gates' decision to study computer science gave her childhood exposure to engineering a direct connection with her own career. She attended Ursuline Academy in Dallas before going to Duke University, where she studied computer science and economics. At the time, computer science was developing rapidly but remained a field in which women were underrepresented. Her choice to enter the discipline placed her directly inside the technological world she had encountered indirectly through her father. She later joined Microsoft, where she worked in areas including product development and management. Her career demonstrated that the exposure she received as a child did not remain simply an interesting family memory. It became part of a trajectory that took her into one of the world's most influential technology companies.The Apollo programme also offered a powerful lesson about collaboration and possibility. Sending astronauts to the Moon required contributions from huge numbers of scientists, engineers, mathematicians and other specialists. The programme demonstrated that seemingly impossible objectives could become achievable when people with different technical skills worked towards the same goal. Growing up around someone involved in the aerospace industry allowed French Gates to see this world at close range. The lesson extended beyond space exploration. Science and technology could be tools for solving problems, creating opportunities and expanding the boundaries of what people believed possible. That understanding would later become important in her own approach to technology and social issues.French Gates has also credited her mother with helping shape her attitude towards education and ambition. Elaine French had not had the opportunity to attend college, and she wanted her children to have access to opportunities that had been unavailable to her. The family's focus on education therefore carried a personal meaning. French Gates was raised with the expectation that she would study, work hard and become self-sufficient. Her parents' different influences complemented one another. Her father provided an example of technical work and introduced his daughters to women working in STEM fields, while her mother emphasised the transformative power of education. Together, these experiences helped establish an early belief that opportunity should be expanded rather than restricted.French Gates eventually moved far beyond her career in computer science and technology. Through her philanthropic work, she became a major advocate for women and girls, focusing on areas including health, economic opportunity and access to education. Her later work has repeatedly returned to the question of what prevents women from reaching their full potential. The childhood experience of meeting women engineers provides an early illustration of why representation can matter. Seeing someone succeed in a field can make that path feel imaginable to the next generation. The women French Gates encountered through her father's workplace showed her that technical careers were possible for women. Decades later, her own work has frequently centred on helping women gain the resources and opportunities needed to pursue their own ambitions.The influence of those company picnics illustrates a broader point about how career aspirations develop. Young people do not learn only through classrooms or textbooks. They also learn from the people they encounter and the possibilities they see around them. French Gates could have grown up thinking of engineering and mathematics as overwhelmingly male professions. Instead, she met women who were already succeeding in those areas. That experience gave substance to the idea that she could enter a technical field herself. It also helped create a connection between representation and opportunity that has remained visible throughout her later advocacy. A role model does not necessarily need to deliver a formal lesson. Sometimes simply seeing someone like yourself succeeding can quietly expand the boundaries of what you believe you can become.French Gates' story ultimately connects three elements that appeared early in her life: technology, education and the visibility of women in technical careers. Her father's aerospace career exposed her to the extraordinary work surrounding the Apollo era, while the women she met through his professional world demonstrated that women could contribute to that work themselves. Her parents' emphasis on education then gave her the foundation to pursue her own academic ambitions. She went on to study computer science, work at Microsoft and eventually devote much of her public life to expanding opportunities for women and girls. The women she encountered at those company gatherings may have been only one part of a much larger set of influences, but they provided a lesson that stayed with her: seeing women succeed can change what the next generation believes is possible.
Article Summary: Melinda French Gates' father worked on NASA's Apollo missions. The women engineers she met became important examples. Company picnics offered her a different view of women's careers. Her parents made education a priority. She eventually chose computer science before going to Duke University.

Article Title: Sea Otters were successfully reintroduced in Canada after their extinction due to fur trade, protecting the kelp populations; but now they are threatening a 'local delicacy'
Article Text:
A flourishing ecosystem

Otters keep the sea urchin population in check with their diet, allowing kelp habitats and the marine life underwater to recover.

An endangered species on the menu

The species is classified as Endangered under the Canadian Species at Risk Act (SARA) because the population has remained severely depleted following a population collapse of more than 75%.

The reintroduction and success of sea otters in British Columbia was a story that initially satisfied everyone including conservationists and the natives. The adorable creatures once occupied much of Canada's Pacific coast, before the fur trade for their exceptionally dense coats turned into a mass death sentence. But now, their population is threatening the availability of a local dish that most around the coast love, according to a report by AS.Hunting of sea otters led to their disappearance from British Columbia by 1929. Years later, between 1969 and 1972, 89 otters were flown south from Alaska and released into Checleset Bay, off Vancouver Island. While the newcomers struggled to settle down initially, their population dropped to around 70 by 1977. After that, however, the recovery gathered remarkable speed. According to a 2022 report by the Government of Canada, the population of sea otters went up from just 3,185 in 2004 to 8,110 in 2017. Not just in numbers, they also spread along the coast.The return of sea otters was more than just the return of a species. These mammals are known for their ferocious appetites, consuming roughly a fifth of their body weight daily.Sea urchins are among their preferred meals, which in turn helps the population of kelp. Without enough predators, the urchins can graze the entire underwater forests into lifeless 'urchin barrens'. Otters keep them in check with their diet, allowing kelp habitats and the marine life underwater to recover.However, their diets are not just limited to urchins. They also eat crabs, clams and northern abalone, a marine snail considered a delicacy and an important traditional food for coastal First Nations. This is where one conservation triumph turns into an ecological concern.Northern abalone have been protected from all harvesting in British Columbia since 1990. Still, their recovery remains extremely slow. Illegal fishing and poor reproduction are considered their biggest problems, and sea otter predation just adds to the pressure. The species is classified as Endangered under the Canadian Species at Risk Act (SARA) because the population has remained severely depleted following a population collapse of more than 75%.One study found 16 times fewer exposed abalone in locations occupied by otters for more than 30 years than in areas the predators had not yet recolonised. Hidden abalone remained more abundant, suggesting the species may survive alongside otters, although at lower densities.Now, the real challenge is deciding how restored nature should live. Saving otters was one plan of action, helping northern abalone coexist with them is another.
Article Summary: Otters are known for their ferocious appetites, consuming roughly a fifth of their body weight daily. They also eat crabs, clams and northern abalone, a marine snail considered a delicacy and an important traditional food for coastal First Nations. The species is classified as Endangered under the Canadian Species at Risk Act (SARA) because the population has remained severely depleted.

Article Title: US army secretary Dan Driscoll steps down amid tensions with Pentagon chief Hegseth: Report
Article Text:
Driscoll’s exit leaves the Army without its Senate-confirmed civilian secretary amid a wider leadership shake-up.

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has resigned after about 18 months in the post, becoming the latest senior military official to leave the Trump administration amid a sweeping shake-up of Pentagon leadership.The White House confirmed Driscoll’s departure on Monday but gave no reason for his resignation. A US Army official said Driscoll had spoken with President Donald Trump about the state of the Army before submitting his resignation. The Wall Street Journal first reported the development.The move comes after months of reported friction between Driscoll and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Driscoll, a close ally of Vice President JD Vance, had previously been seen as a rising figure within the administration and, at one point, as a potential alternative to Hegseth.The White House, however, praised Driscoll’s tenure, saying he had helped advance Trump’s defence agenda, strengthen Army readiness and lethality, support military operations and assist with US efforts to negotiate an end to the Russia-Ukraine war, reported AP.Driscoll’s resignation comes against the backdrop of an unusually turbulent period for the US Army and the wider Pentagon.In April, Hegseth abruptly removed Army Chief of Staff Gen.Randy George, the service’s highest-ranking uniformed officer, along with two other senior generals. No detailed public explanation was given for the removals. Driscoll later described George as a “transformational leader” and told lawmakers that he and his family had gone to George’s home after his departure.Two months later, Gen Christopher Donahue, who headed US Army Europe and Africa, also left his post after an effort to extend his tenure failed. Donahue had served only about 18 months in the role and was regarded as one of the Army’s senior combat leaders.The churn has extended beyond the Army. Navy secretary John Phelan was forced out in April after reported clashes with Hegseth and his deputy, becoming the first head of a US military service to leave during Trump’s second term. Hegseth has also removed or pushed out numerous other senior generals and admirals since taking charge of the Pentagon.Driscoll had positioned himself as an advocate of faster military modernisation, particularly as cheap drones and counter-drone technology reshape warfare.He pushed for cutting bureaucratic delays in defence procurement and encouraged military units to develop and field new drone capabilities more quickly. But some of the initiatives he championed have since been rolled back.Under Gen Christopher LaNeve, who took over as the Army’s acting chief of staff after George’s removal, the service has moved to end a drone-modernisation effort that Driscoll had supported.Driscoll also took on an unusual diplomatic role for an Army secretary, becoming involved in the Trump administration’s efforts to broker an end to the Russia-Ukraine war.An Iraq War veteran and former tech investor, Driscoll served as an Army armour officer before entering Republican politics and later becoming an adviser to Vance. Trump nominated him in 2024, describing him as a “disruptor and change agent.” The Senate confirmed him in February 2025.His exit now adds another major name to a rapidly changing Pentagon leadership structure under Hegseth, with the Army experiencing some of the most significant turnover.
Article Summary: Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has resigned after about 18 months in the post. He is the latest senior military official to leave the Trump administration amid a sweeping shake-up of Pentagon leadership. The White House confirmed his departure but gave no reason for his resignation.

Article Title: ChatGPT is first AI chatbot to face tougher EU rules
Article Text:
ChatGPT is first AI chatbot to face tougher EU rules﻿

ChatGPT will have to comply with tougher safety rules after the EU added it Monday to a list of digital services subject to greater legal scrutiny, a first for an AI chatbot.Brussels also designated Reddit and Roblox as “very large” online platforms, a label that comes with additional obligations and oversight. “ChatGPT, Reddit and Roblox will now be held to a higher standard of scrutiny and accountability in the EU, in line with their large impact on our citizens and society,” EU technology chief Henna Virkkunen said.The designation applies to platforms and search engines with over 45 million monthly active users in the 27-nation bloc, a threshold the three platforms reported meeting, the commission said. The three now have four months to comply with additional obligations under the Digital Services Act, a content law the EU has deployed to rein in Big Tech.
