Article Title: In 1985, Harrison Ford began protecting 389 acres of his 800-acre Wyoming ranch from development, preserving a migration corridor for elk and mule deer
Article Text:
Ford was looking for a place outside Los Angeles in the early 1980s | Wikimedia Commons/Kevin Paul

Ford was looking for a place outside Los Angeles in the early 1980s | Wikimedia Commons/Kevin Paul

Ford chose the entire 800-acre property

Conservation easements changed what could be built

389 acres were placed in perpetual protection

Los Angeles Times

Los Angeles Times

The land became part of Ford's conservation work

Elk in the wild | Wikimedia Commons

Elk and mule deer still depend on connected habitat

Harrison Ford bought an 800-acre property in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, after he decided that the valley suited him better than Sun Valley. Elk and mule deer already moved across the ranch, while bald eagles, blue herons and native cutthroat trout occupied parts of the property. Ford later began placing conservation easements on the land to limit development. By the 1990s, 389 acres of Ford’s ranch had been placed into a perpetual conservation easement, and the arrangement prevented the protected portion from being developed and kept the land available as wildlife habitat.Ford and his then-wife, Melissa Mathison, were looking for a place outside Los Angeles in the early 1980s, and initially considered properties around Sun Valley before turning their attention to Jackson Hole. The property they eventually selected covered 800 acres along the Snake River. The Land Report says migrating elk and mule deer used the pastures, while the property also supported bald eagles, blue herons and native cutthroat trout.Ford had the option of buying only the existing house and a small surrounding parcel, but instead purchased the entire tract. He designed the main house later while working in Paris on the film Frantic, sending instructions to workers in Wyoming.A 1994 Los Angeles Times profile described the property as an 800-acre ranch with a family compound, guest cottages, a workshop and areas of spruce, aspen and hawthorn.Ford began donating conservation easements on his property in 1985, according to the Land Report. The easements prohibited substantial development or other development that would impair wildlife and natural resources on the protected portions of the ranch. A conservation easement places permanent restrictions on how the land can be developed, and in Jackson Hole, such easements have become an important tool for keeping private parcels connected to surrounding wildlife habitat. The Jackson Hole Land Trust now says conservation easements are particularly important in Teton County because private land is concentrated on the valley floor, where wildlife depends on open areas and connected habitat.Ford had placed 389 acres of his 800-acre ranch into perpetual trust as wildlife habitat by August 1994, according to the. The newspaper reported that Ford planned to use only a few additional small areas for possible homes for his children. The protected acreage represented nearly half of the ranch, which also covered land that wildlife already used. Thedescribed elk and other animals that moved through the property, while the Land Report specifically noted the presence of migrating elk and mule deer. Conservation easements were still relatively uncommon when Ford's decision came, and the Land Report quoted Stephen Small, who helped write the federal tax provisions governing conservation easements, as saying that the Jackson Hole Land Trust was an early pioneer in the field.Ford was interested in protecting the ranch for broader involvement in environmental conservation, and he served on the board of Conservation International and later became vice chair of the organization. XPRIZE's biography of Ford notes that he donated 389 acres of his Wyoming property to the Jackson Hole Land Trust for a conservation easement. It also describes his long involvement with Conservation International and its biodiversity programs.The Land Report said Ford's conservation work on his own property was closely connected to his interest in environmental protection elsewhere. His Jackson Hole ranch, however, provided a direct way to restrict development on land where wildlife was already moving.Elk and mule deer move between seasonal ranges across a mixture of public and private land, which make undeveloped private parcels important where they connect larger habitat areas. The Wyoming Wildlife Federation identifies migration corridors as critical areas that allow elk, mule deer and other ungulates to move between summer and winter ranges.Ford's 389-acre easement has a rather narrow role: it permanently restricts development on part of an 800-acre private ranch that lies within a landscape used by wildlife. The Jackson Hole Land Trust currently lists more than 20,000 acres of protected land in the Jackson Hole area, with elk, moose, mule deer and pronghorn among the wildlife species associated with those conservation areas.
Article Summary: Harrison Ford bought an 800-acre property in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, after he decided that the valley suited him better than Sun Valley. Elk and mule deer already moved across the ranch, while bald eagles, blue herons and native cutthroat trout occupied parts of the property. Ford later began placing conservation easements on the land to limit development.

Article Title: In 1968–1969, Robert Redford acquired a Utah ski area and surrounding land amid development pressure; his family later placed 865 acres of wildlife habitat under permanent protection
Article Text:
Ski lift at Sundance Mountain Resort. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid

From Timp Haven to

Sundance Mountain Resort

Rustic accounting office at Sundance Mountain Resort. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

The 865-acre conservation easement by the Redford family

The protection expanded after the original easement

In the late 1960s, when Robert Redford turned his attention to Timp Haven, a small ski area in Utah’s Provo Canyon, the surrounding landscape was facing pressure from development. Sundance Institute's corporate archives show that in 1961, Redford first encountered the canyon when he purchased two acres and built a cabin near Mount Timpanogos. Several years later, he acquired thousands of additional acres and, in August 1968, purchased the entire Timp Haven ski operation. The next year, Redford renamed the property Sundance, the mountain resort and community named after his role in the filmWhile modern resort retrospectives simplify this milestone to a single 1969 opening date, a closer cross-reference of land management records and Ski Utah ’s historical records mention that he purchased the existing Timp Haven operation in August 1968. Together, the separate records show a transition that unfolded across two years rather than a single transaction in 1969.Redford’s decision to acquire the property was influenced by concerns about how the canyon could be developed. Ski Utah’s history reported that in the late 1960s he acquired around 3,000 acres in an effort to prevent a proposed housing development of A-frame cabins on small parcels from being built in the canyon.Subsequently, he purchased Timp Haven itself and pursued a different model for the mountain, one that included recreation with preservation of the surrounding landscape.The Stewart family developed Timp Haven in the 1940s, and the operation expanded over the following years. By the time Redford purchased it, the resort already had lifts and other ski infrastructure. Therefore, his role was not to create skiing in the canyon from scratch, but to take over the existing operations and reshape its future.Redford chose a different approach from intensive mountain development, as he intended to develop little and preserve a great deal. The archives notes that when Redford purchased the land, he redesignated a large majority of it as wilderness preserve. Consequently, the resort’s conservation philosophy developed alongside its recreational infrastructure instead of requiring the ski area to disappear. The institute recorded the 1969 acquisition at 5,000 acres, and the resort subsequently described Sundance as a destination set within those acres of preserved wilderness.The Sundance area lies on the southeastern flank of Mount Timpanogos and contains forests, meadows, wetlands and streams. Furthermore, snowmelt from the mountains feeds waterways that flow toward the North Fork of the Provo River, thus giving the region an important watershed role alongside its wildlife and recreational value.In 1997, the Redford family donated a permanent conservation easement covering 865 acres to Utah Open Lands . The permanent deed describes the Redford Family Nature and Wildlife Preserve as more than 860 acres of critical wildlife habitat, vital watershed and undisturbed alpine meadows protected in perpetuity.The contract explains that such an easement is different from donating the land itself, as it is a binding legal agreement that restricts development while the property can remain in private ownership. In this case, the easement ensured that the protected acreage's conservation value would remain safeguarded even as ownership or use of its surrounding landscape could change in future.The preserve lies above the Sundance property in North Fork Canyon and includes habitat and watershed resources that the organisation considers important. The protected landscape is reportedly used by wildlife such as elk, mule deer, moose, cougar and black bear, as well as numerous bird species.The conservation efforts by the Redford family continued for decades following the original 865-acre easement. In 2020, Utah Open Lands protected another 316.5 acres through the Redford Family Elk Meadows Preserve. The property reportedly contains year-round moose habitat, important elk habitat, wetlands and areas used by black bears, cougars and coyotes.The latter protection highlights the continuity in the family’s approach to the landscape. The 1997 easement established permanent protection for one major block of habitat, while the later agreement added another area with important wetlands and wildlife habitat.Meanwhile, the resort itself continued to evolve. In 2020, Redford sold Sundance Mountain Resort, and the new ownership vowed to maintain the balance between responsible development and land preservation associated with the resort’s history. The change in ownership did not erase the conservation commitments established during Redford’s tenure. Today, the Redford Family Nature and Wildlife Preserve represents the most concrete permanent protection associated with the family’s early conservation efforts at Sundance.
Article Summary: Robert Redford purchased Timp Haven, a small ski area in Utah’s Provo Canyon, in 1968. The next year, Redford renamed the property Sundance, the mountain resort and community named after his role in the film Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid. In 1997, the Redford family donated a permanent conservation easement covering 865 acres to Utah Open Lands. The protected landscape is reportedly used by wildlife such as elk, mule deer, moose, cougar and black bear, as well as numerous bird species.

Article Title: In 1996, CNN founder Ted Turner bought a reported 558,000-acre New Mexico ranch; conservation work expanded its bison herd and restored about 30 miles of streams
Article Text:
Vermejo Headquarters aerial view. Image credits: Ted Turner Reserves

A working ranch begins a long restoration effort

An image of an American bison. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

.

More than 1,200 bison have been restored in the landscape

Conservation expanded beyond the ranch’s bison restoration

In 1996, when CNN founder Ted Turner bought Vermejo Park Ranch from Pennzoil, he acquired an enormous private landscape in northern New Mexico and southern Colorado that had a long history of ranching, mining and intensive land uses. Reported to cover roughly 558,000 acres by High Country News, the property contains diverse habitat, ranging from semi-arid grasslands to alpine forests, that support vital populations of bison, elk, black bears and mountain lions. Over the decades that followed, Turner’s managers worked to restore parts of the overused landscape, with the ranch’s bison population eventually exceeding 1,200 animals and riparian areas along around 30 miles of streams undergoing restoration.Ted Turner’s conservation interests predated the Vermejo purchase, as he had already begun acquiring large Western ranches and building bison herds, but the newly acquired landscape gave him an unusually large area on which wildlife conservation, ranching and habitat restoration could occur simultaneously. The ranch was not converted into a conventional nature preserve; instead, the management approach opted to maintain productive uses while changing land-management practices to improve habitat and protect native species.This was reportedly a part of Turner’s broader effort to combine conservation with economic activity on his private ranches.High Country News described the property as overgrazed and overused and noted that the managers worked over many years to restore its ecological conditions. Furthermore, the size of the property allowed restoration work to take place across grasslands, forests, streams and wetlands while the ranch continued to operate as a working landscape. NASA DEVELOP technical report , produced with Vermejo Ranch and Colorado Parks and Wildlife, noted that the ranch partnered with the US Fish and Wildlife Service and Colorado Parks and Wildlife on a large native-trout restoration project. Beginning in 2002, the work included wetland and riparian restoration and reintroduction of Rio Grande cutthroat trout in the Costilla Creek watershed. Additionally, the project used satellite and other remote sensing data to identify wetland and riparian regions where additional habitat restoration could be undertaken.The ranch’s conservation agreements also brought state and federal agencies into long-term habitat work in 2013. Notably, because Costilla Creek acts as an interstate waterway, the native trout restoration initiatives spanned a shared watershed matrixThe New Mexico Department of Game and Fish reported that the park ranch, the department, Colorado Parks and Wildlife and the US Fish and Wildlife Service jointly signed an agreement to safeguard the Rio Grande cutthroat trout. The initiative included removing non-native trout in parts of the watershed while allowing the ranch to continue agricultural and recreational uses.Bison became one of the most visible symbols of Turner’s conservation efforts. The CNN founder considered the species both an important part of the Great Plains ecosystem and a practical component of large-scale ranch management. At Vermejo, the restoration programme eventually brought the bison population to more than 1,200 animals.Independent academic research shed additional light on the size of the herd. A 2024 University of Nebraska-Lincoln master’s thesis examined the spatial ecology of American bison on Vermejo Park Ranch and documented a population of around 1,200 bison during 2022-23. The research analysed how bison movements and grazing patterns related to forage and landscape conditions on the ranch. Additionally, early conservation reports documented the restoration of riparian areas along about 30 miles of streams, while NASA and government records verify long-term wetland stability and provide satellite imaging confirmation of these remote mountain ecosystems.In 1997, Turner established the Turner Endangered Species Fund, which subsequently supported conservation projects that involved species like Mexican wolves and black-footed ferrets. Some of those projects occurred on Vermejo, while others were undertaken on Turner’s other ranches.Additionally, the ranch remained economically active, as activities like hunting, fishing, tourism and ranching continued alongside conservation work. According to the US Fish and Wildlife Service , the property contains 19 fishable lakes and more than 550,000 acres of habitat, while the ranch’s current materials describe about 30 miles of streams and a range of wildlife-based recreational opportunities.The restoration work continued beyond the earliest years of Turner’s ownership. In 2021, the CNN founder established the Turner Institute of Ecoagriculture, thus extending his interest in combining ecological restoration with productive land management.By the time of recent reporting, the property had become a long-running example of private conservation on a working landscape. Its transformation was not a single before-and-after event; instead, it involved changes to land use, restoration of riparian and wetland habitats, native fish recovery, reclamation of areas affected by historic mining and long-term management of a large bison herd.
Article Summary: CNN founder Ted Turner bought Vermejo Park Ranch from Pennzoil in 1996. The property is in northern New Mexico and southern Colorado and covers 558,000 acres. Over the decades that followed, Turner’s managers worked to restore parts of the overused landscape. The restoration programme eventually brought the bison population to more than 1,200 animals.

Article Title: Laurene Powell Jobs left Wall Street and moved to Florence for eight months, then built a multibillion-dollar empire funding education, climate and social change
Article Text:
Why Laurene Powell Jobs left Wall Street and moved to Florence

How she met Steve Jobs and built a life beyond finance

Emerson Collective became the centre of her social-impact work

How education became one of her biggest priorities

Her fortune expanded dramatically after Steve Jobs' death

Why she invested heavily in media

Climate change became another major focus

She also became involved in immigration and social justice

Powell Jobs expanded her influence beyond philanthropy

From Wall Street to a different kind of power

Laurene Powell Jobs took an unconventional route from Wall Street to becoming one of the most influential philanthropists and investors in the United States. After graduating from the University of Pennsylvania in 1985, she spent a year at Merrill Lynch and two years at Goldman Sachs before leaving finance and moving to Florence, Italy, where she lived for eight months. She later returned to the US and earned an MBA from Stanford University in 1991. Her life changed dramatically after she married Apple co-founder Steve Jobs and later inherited a substantial fortune following his death in 2011. Rather than simply preserving that wealth, Powell Jobs channelled it into Emerson Collective, an organisation involved in education, immigration, climate, media and social change, turning her personal fortune into a far-reaching platform for influence.Powell Jobs was born in West Milford, New Jersey, in 1963 and experienced financial hardship early in life after her father, a Marine Corps pilot, died in a plane crash when she was three. Her mother was left to raise three children, and Powell Jobs later recalled learning the importance of becoming self-sufficient. She attended the University of Pennsylvania, where she studied political science and economics, graduating in 1985.She then entered the financial world, working for a year at Merrill Lynch and two years in Goldman Sachs' fixed-income division. Although the experience gave her valuable exposure to finance, she eventually became dissatisfied with the sense that her work was not contributing enough to the wider world. She left Goldman Sachs and moved to Florence, where she spent eight months before returning to the United States and enrolling at Stanford Graduate School of Business. She earned her MBA in 1991, the same year she married Steve Jobs.Powell Jobs met Steve Jobs while attending a lecture he was giving at Stanford's business school. According to accounts later included in Walter Isaacson's biography of Jobs, the two ended up sitting beside each other and began talking. They went to dinner after the lecture and their relationship developed quickly. Jobs proposed on New Year's Day in 1990, and the couple married in 1991. They eventually had three children, Reed, Erin and Eve. Powell Jobs stepped back from a conventional professional career for a period to focus on raising her family, while also pursuing entrepreneurial and social-impact interests. She started Terravera, a small business producing organic meals, although the venture did not last. Her interest in education became more enduring. In 1997, she and Carlos Watson co-founded College Track, a nonprofit designed to help students from disadvantaged backgrounds complete high school, attend college and graduate. The organisation reflected a personal belief that education could fundamentally alter a young person's opportunities.Powell Jobs began laying the groundwork for Emerson Collective in 2004, years before Steve Jobs died. The organisation eventually became the principal vehicle through which she pursued philanthropy, investment and advocacy. Emerson Collective describes its mission around creating greater opportunity and addressing entrenched social problems, with work spanning education, immigration, climate change, media and other areas. Its structure is unusual because it operates as a limited liability company rather than solely as a traditional charitable foundation. That gives Powell Jobs greater flexibility to combine grants and philanthropic activity with investments in companies and other organisations. The model means her activities cannot be understood simply as charitable giving. Some of the money is directed towards nonprofits and social causes, while other capital is invested in businesses, media organisations and projects that align with her broader objectives. This approach has made Emerson Collective an unusually flexible instrument for deploying a vast personal fortune.Education has remained one of the central themes of Powell Jobs' work. Her involvement began well before she inherited Steve Jobs' fortune, with the creation of College Track in 1997. The organisation works with students from communities that face barriers to higher education, supporting them through high school and college. She later backed other education initiatives through Emerson Collective, including XQ, a major programme focused on transforming high-school education in the United States. XQ has supported schools and educators seeking to rethink how high-school students learn and prepare for life after graduation. Powell Jobs has repeatedly argued that education needs new approaches and greater experimentation, drawing on the problem-solving mindset associated with entrepreneurship. Her own educational journey, from a financially constrained childhood to Penn and Stanford, has also helped shape the importance she places on creating opportunities for young people who might otherwise struggle to access them.Steve Jobs died on October 5, 2011, after years of health problems. His death transformed Powell Jobs' financial position as she became the beneficiary of a substantial portfolio of Apple and Disney holdings. The precise value of her inheritance has varied over time and depends heavily on the valuation date, particularly because both companies' share prices have changed dramatically. Jobs had received a large Disney stake when Disney acquired Pixar in 2006, while the family's Apple holdings also represented a major source of wealth. Powell Jobs consequently became one of the world's wealthiest women. Her post-2011 activities showed that she intended to use that financial power actively rather than simply hold the assets. Emerson Collective expanded considerably, giving her the ability to direct capital towards causes and organisations while also taking positions in commercial ventures. Her wealth therefore became not just a private financial asset but a mechanism through which she could influence education, journalism, climate policy, immigration and other areas of public life.One of the most visible parts of Powell Jobs' expansion has been her involvement in media. Emerson Collective acquired a majority stake in Atlantic Media, the company behind The Atlantic, in 2017. She also became involved with other media and entertainment ventures, including Pop-Up Magazine Productions and Concordia Studio, while investing in or supporting organisations involved in journalism and documentary storytelling. Her interest in media fits closely with her broader belief in the power of storytelling to influence public debate. Through these investments, Powell Jobs gained influence not only as a philanthropist but also as an important participant in the American media landscape. The strategy also reflects a distinctive feature of Emerson Collective's model. Rather than separating charitable activity from commercial investment completely, the organisation can use different forms of capital depending on the objective. That flexibility has allowed Powell Jobs to support journalism and storytelling while also participating directly in the businesses producing them.Climate change is another major area in which Powell Jobs has directed resources through Emerson Collective. The organisation has supported efforts related to environmental protection, climate solutions and efforts to address the wider consequences of climate change. Her approach has generally involved backing organisations, entrepreneurs and initiatives that seek structural changes rather than limiting support to traditional charitable programmes. This fits the wider philosophy behind Emerson Collective, which attempts to combine philanthropy with investment and advocacy. The scale of Powell Jobs' wealth gives her the ability to support projects for long periods and to take risks that conventional funding models may not always accommodate. Her climate work therefore sits alongside her education and media interests as part of a broader strategy of using private capital to influence areas that she believes require significant change.Immigration and social justice have formed another significant part of Powell Jobs' public work. Emerson Collective has supported organisations working with immigrants and communities affected by policy changes, while Powell Jobs herself has spoken publicly about social inequality and political issues. Her involvement has extended beyond writing cheques, with the organisation supporting advocacy groups and initiatives designed to influence public discussion and policy. She has also used high-profile appearances and conversations with activists to bring attention to issues she considers important. This combination of funding, advocacy and media influence has made her considerably more visible than she was during Steve Jobs' lifetime. Before his death, Powell Jobs largely maintained a private profile and was often described publicly primarily in relation to her husband. In the years since, she has developed a distinct identity as a philanthropist, investor and advocate with considerable influence of her own.Her activities have also reached the world of professional sport. In 2017, Powell Jobs invested a reported $500 million for a roughly 20% stake in Monumental Sports & Entertainment, the company that owns the NBA's Washington Wizards, WNBA's Washington Mystics and operates Capital One Arena. The investment added another major sector to her portfolio and demonstrated the breadth of her financial interests. Her influence has consequently extended across education, media, entertainment, climate, social policy and professional sport. Yet the scale of her activities has also attracted scrutiny. Because Emerson Collective is structured as an LLC, it has more flexibility and fewer disclosure requirements than a conventional private foundation. That makes it difficult for outsiders to determine the full extent of Powell Jobs' giving and investments. Supporters argue that the structure allows her to respond quickly to changing circumstances, while critics have questioned the transparency that comes with such a model.Powell Jobs' journey is unusual because her transformation did not happen overnight. Her decision to leave Wall Street and spend eight months in Florence came decades before she became one of the world's wealthiest women. Her early interest in education, her experience raising a family and her work with College Track all predated the enormous fortune she later inherited. Steve Jobs' death undoubtedly changed the scale of what she could do, but it did not create her interest in social issues from scratch. Through Emerson Collective, she has since combined wealth with philanthropy, investment, advocacy and media ownership in a way that gives her unusual freedom to pursue causes she considers important. Her story is therefore not simply about inheriting billions. It is about how a woman who once left finance because she wanted her work to have greater meaning eventually gained the resources to decide, on an enormous scale, what that meaningful work would look like.
Article Summary: Laurene Powell Jobs was born in 1963 in West Milford, New Jersey. She studied political science and economics at the University of Pennsylvania. She spent a year at Merrill Lynch and two years at Goldman Sachs before leaving finance and moving to Florence, Italy. She later returned to the US and earned an MBA from Stanford University in 1991. Her life changed dramatically after she married Apple co-founder Steve Jobs and later inherited a substantial fortune following his death in 2011. She channelled it into Emerson Collective, an organisation involved in education, immigration, climate, media and social change.

Article Title: A Missouri man bought the 1914 mansion his late wife had always loved to save it from redevelopment; restoration later revealed $150,000 worth of hidden damage
Article Text:
Photo: comobusinesstimes.com

A house tied to a love story

Buying to save, not to flip

The moment the real work began

The $150,000 surprise

Balancing preservation and practicality

Why houses like this matter

Lessons for anyone considering a historic home

A home with a future

Poll Vote & Share your view What aspect of 'The Belle of West Broadway' do you find most appealing? Architectural Design Historical Significance Love Story Behind It 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

When Fred Parry’s late wife, Mary, first saw the stately 1914 mansion on West Broadway in Columbia, Missouri, she fell in love. Years later, after her death, Parry found himself facing a choice: let the historic home be redeveloped or step in to save it. He chose the latter, buying the property with the goal of preserving its character and restoring it as a single-family residence. But as crews began peeling back layers of paint and plaster, they uncovered far more damage than anyone had anticipated: rotted framing, compromised structural members and other issues that would eventually add about $150,000 to the restoration bill. His story, as told to the Columbia Business Times, is part love letter to a house, part cautionary tale about historic renovation. Read on to know more:The mansion, known locally as 'The Belle of West Broadway', sits on a prominent corner just west of downtown Columbia. Built in 1914, it features classic early-20th-century details: tall columns, wide porches, high ceilings, hardwood floors and ornate woodwork that reflect the craftsmanship of the era.For Mary Parry, the house was more than just architecture. She had long admired it and often spoke about how much she loved its design and presence on the street. After she passed away, Fred Parry found himself drawn back to the property, not only as a preservation project but as a way to honour her memory.When the house came up for sale, Parry knew there was interest from developers who might convert it into apartments or split the lot. Rather than risk losing its historic character, he decided to buy it himself with the intention of restoring it as a single-family home and keeping its original footprint intact.His plan was not to create a perfect museum piece, but a liveable home that respected the building’s history while meeting modern standards for comfort and safety. That meant keeping key features, such as the grand staircase, original mouldings and fireplace surrounds, while updating systems like electrical, plumbing and insulation.Like many historic renovations, the project started with optimism and a budget based on what could be seen during walkthroughs and inspections. But once contractors began opening walls, removing old additions and stripping away decades of paint and patchwork, the true condition of the house emerged.Crews discovered things like: Rotted wood framing in key structural areas; compromised floor joists and beams that needed reinforcement or replacement;water damage that had spread further than surface signs suggested; and outdated and potentially unsafe electrical and plumbing runs hidden behind walls.What had looked like a straightforward restoration quickly turned into a major structural rehabilitation.Parry estimates that the hidden damage uncovered during restoration added roughly $150,000 to the overall cost of the project. That sum went toward: replacing and reinforcing structural members to ensure the house was sound; addressing long-term water intrusion and moisture issues; and upgrading systems to meet current building codes while minimising impact on historic features.For a homeowner operating on a fixed budget, that kind of mid-project escalation is stressful. But Parry says he never considered cutting corners. “If you’re going to do this, you do it right,” he told the Columbia Business Times, reflecting the mindset of many historic preservationists who see themselves as stewards rather than flippers.Restoring a 110-year-old mansion is not just about fixing what’s broken; it’s about making choices that balance historical integrity with modern living. In the Belle of West Broadway, that has meant: Preserving original woodwork, doors and hardware wherever possible; repairing rather than replacing historic windows when feasible; adding insulation and weatherproofing in ways that don’t damage character-defining features; and designing kitchens and bathrooms that feel contemporary but respect the scale and style of the house.The goal is for the home to function well for today’s occupants while still feeling like a 1914 mansion when you walk through the front door.For Columbia, the Belle of West Broadway is more than one man’s project. It’s part of a small but significant collection of early-20th-century homes that give the city’s older neighbourhoods their character. When houses like this are demolished or radically altered, the streetscape changes in ways that can’t easily be reversed.Parry’s decision to buy and restore the mansion helps keep that architectural heritage intact. It also sets an example for other owners of historic properties, showing that preservation is possible even when the costs and challenges are significant.Parry’s experience offers several takeaways for anyone thinking about buying and restoring an older house:Expect the unexpected. Even thorough inspections can miss problems hidden behind walls and under floors.Budget for contingencies. A common rule of thumb is to set aside 10–20% of the projected renovation cost for surprises; in very old homes, that may still be conservative.Work with contractors who understand historic construction. Techniques and materials used a century ago don’t always align with modern building practices, and inexperienced crews can inadvertently cause more damage.Be clear on your goals. Are you aiming for a museum-quality restoration, a comfortable family home with historic character, or something in between? Your answer will guide countless decisions.As restoration work continues, the Belle of West Broadway is slowly returning to the kind of condition its original builders would recognise, while gaining the updates needed for another century of use. For Fred Parry, the project is both a labour of love and a tribute to his late wife, whose admiration for the house helped set everything in motion.In a time when many older homes are torn down or stripped of their character, this mansion’s survival is a small but meaningful victory for preservation. And for anyone who drives past West Broadway and notices the fresh paint, repaired porches and cared-for gardens, it’s a reminder that behind every historic house there’s often a story of someone who chose to save it.
Article Summary: Fred Parry bought the 1914 mansion on West Broadway in Columbia, Missouri, to restore it as a single-family home. The restoration cost $150,000 and involved replacing and reinforcing structural members, addressing long-term water intrusion and moisture issues. Parry says he never considered cutting corners and that the project is a cautionary tale about historic renovation.

Article Title: Scientists used geothermal drill-hole temperatures in Oregon’s Cascades and found at least 81 cubic kilometres of water hidden in volcanic rock, nearly 3 times Lake Mead’s capacity
Article Text:
Oregon’s Cascade Range(Representative image by Canva)

A surprise hidden in old drill data

How much water are we talking about?

Oregon’s Cascade RangePhoto: Canva

Why volcanic mountains can store so much water

Implications for water budgets and drought resilience

Connections to volcanic hazards

A new way to “see” groundwater

What this means for the Oregon Cascades

Poll Vote & Share your view What aspect of this discovery do you find most intriguing? The volume of water stored The method of discovery Implications for volcanic activity The complexity of water storage 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A hidden resource with big questions

Beneath the forested slopes of Oregon’s Cascade Range, scientists have uncovered a vast, hidden reservoir of water locked inside volcanic rock. By analysing temperature data from geothermal drill holes, a University of Oregon-led team estimated that at least 81 cubic kilometres of water are stored in the region’s subsurface, nearly three times the capacity of Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States. The discovery, announced by the university , reshapes how researchers think about water storage in volcanic mountains and could have implications for everything from regional water budgets to volcanic hazard assessment.The finding did not come from new drilling or expensive field campaigns, but from a fresh look at existing data. The team, led by University of Oregon geosciences professor Leif Karlstrom, focused on temperature measurements collected from geothermal exploration wells drilled decades ago across the Oregon Cascades.These drill holes were originally used to assess geothermal energy potential, not to map groundwater. But the researchers realised that the way heat moves through rock is strongly influenced by whether the pores and fractures are filled with air or water. Water conducts heat differently than dry rock, and those differences leave a detectable signature in temperature profiles.By modelling how heat should flow through dry volcanic rock and comparing it to the actual temperature logs, the scientists could infer where large volumes of water must be present.The result was a surprising picture of the subsurface: instead of mostly dry, fractured lava flows, the team found evidence for a regionally extensive, water-saturated zone stretching across a large portion of the Oregon Cascades.The team’s calculations suggest that at least 81 cubic kilometres of water are stored in the volcanic rocks of the study area. To put that in perspective, Lake Mead, the massive reservoir formed by Hoover Dam on the Colorado River, has a full capacity of about 28 cubic kilometres. In other words, the hidden aquifer beneath the Oregon Cascades could hold nearly three times as much water as the largest reservoir in the U.S.This does not mean there is an underground “lake” that could be tapped like a surface reservoir. The water is dispersed through countless pores, fractures and vesicles (gas bubbles) in layers of lava flows, volcaniclastic deposits and other volcanic rocks. It is more like a giant, three-dimensional sponge than a single body of standing water.Volcanic terrains are unusually good at storing groundwater. Repeated eruptions build up thick stacks of lava flows, ash layers and fragmented volcanic deposits. As these materials cool and weather, they develop: Porous zones where gas bubbles were trapped in solidifying lava; fracture networks created by cooling, tectonic stress and later erosion; and permeable layers of volcanic breccia and sediment between harder flows.In wet, high-elevation environments like the Oregon Cascades, abundant precipitation from rain and snowmelt can infiltrate deeply into these rocks. Eventually, this forms large saturated zones which can last for long periods, even during dry summers or multi-year droughts.Many previous models assumed that a large fraction of water in volcanic mountains either drained rapidly through fractures or was stored primarily in shallow soils and alluvial valleys. The new results indicate that a much larger fraction is stored in the volcanic bedrock itself, with important implications for water movement through the landscape.This finding raises a key question for water managers and hydrologists: How much of the precipitation that falls on the Cascades is stored in these deep volcanic aquifers, and how slowly is it released? If a significant portion of runoff is buffered by this hidden storage, it could mean that streams and springs are more resilient to drought than previously thought, supported by slow drainage from the volcanic aquifer. It also suggests that regional water budgets may need to be revised to account for larger subsurface storage and longer residence times. And climate change impacts on streamflow could be moderated, at least temporarily, by the slow release of water from these deep reservoirs.At the same time, the study underscores how little is still known about groundwater in many mountainous regions. The Oregon Cascades are relatively well studied compared to other ranges, yet a water store of this magnitude remained undetected until now.The findings also matter for volcanology. Water plays a critical role in how volcanoes behave.When magma rises through wet crust, it can interact with groundwater, potentially triggering explosive eruptions or hydrothermal activity.Knowing that large volumes of water are stored in the volcanic edifice itself helps scientists better model: How heat and fluids move beneath active volcanoes; where hydrothermal systems are likely to form; and how eruptions might interact with subsurface water to produce phreatic or phreatomagmatic explosions.While the study does not change the overall hazard profile of Oregon’s volcanoes, it adds an important piece to the puzzle of how these systems are plumbed.One of the most powerful aspects of this work is the method itself. Instead of relying solely on traditional groundwater monitoring wells, which are sparse in remote mountain areas, the team used existing geothermal temperature logs as a kind of indirect imaging tool.This approach could be applied in other volcanic regions around the world, from the Andes to the Japanese archipelago, where similar stacks of lava flows and abundant precipitation may hide large aquifers. It offers a relatively low-cost way to refine estimates of subsurface water storage in places where drilling new wells would be prohibitively expensive.For the Oregon Cascades, the study suggests that the landscape’s water cycle is more complex and more buffered than previously recognised. The forests, meadows and rivers that define the region are underpinned by a vast, slow-moving reservoir that helps regulate flow through wet and dry periods.The researchers emphasise that this is a minimum estimate; the true volume could be larger as more data are analysed and models are refined. Future work will likely focus on: Integrating the temperature-based estimates with streamflow, geochemical and seismic data; mapping how the aquifer varies across different volcanic centres and rock types; assessing how climate change might affect recharge and long-term storage in these systems.The discovery of 81 cubic kilometres of water beneath the Oregon Cascades is a reminder of how much remains unknown about Earth’s subsurface. While this water is not a direct source of drinking water or irrigation in the conventional sense, it plays a crucial role in sustaining ecosystems, streams and potentially even geothermal resources. As scientists continue to probe these hidden reservoirs, the challenge will be to understand not just how much water is there, but how it moves, how it interacts with surface systems and how it might respond to a warming, changing climate.
Article Summary: University of Oregon-led team estimated that at least 81 cubic kilometres of water are stored in the region’s subsurface. This is nearly three times the capacity of Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States. The discovery could have implications for everything from regional water budgets to volcanic hazard assessment.

Article Title: Watch: Woman with mental health history charges at NYPD officers with kitchen knives before being shot
Article Text:
The dramatic confrontation unfolded near an NYPD substation outside One Times Square, where officers spent several minutes attempting to persuade the woman to put down the weapons

A woman who stabbed two people in New York City's Times Square before being shot by police charged at officers wielding two kitchen knives and refused repeated demands to surrender, authorities said. The investigators ruled out any immediate indication that the attack was terrorism-related.The 49-year-old Queens woman was confronted by NYPD officers shortly after stabbing a 32-year-old woman and a 68-year-old man on Monday afternoon. The younger woman died from her injuries, while the man remained in stable condition.The dramatic confrontation unfolded near an NYPD substation outside One Times Square, where officers spent several minutes attempting to persuade the woman to put down the weapons, Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said.The woman instead told officers, “I’m not dropping anything, I would rather kill both of you,” Tisch said.Police then used a Taser, but it failed to incapacitate her. Video recorded by bystanders showed the woman subsequently moving towards the officers while waving the knives.Two officers opened fire, striking the woman. She fell to the ground and was handcuffed by police, while officers administered first aid.She was later pronounced dead.Despite the apparently random nature of the attack and the violent confrontation that followed, police said there was no evidence to suggest that the incident was a terrorist attack.Tisch said the woman had a “documented mental health history with the NYPD”, including incidents in 2018 and 2019. She did not have an arrest history with the department, and police have not disclosed further details about her mental health history.The attack began when the woman pulled two knives from a shopping bag and stabbed the 68-year-old man in the abdomen as he waited to cross the street with his wife after emerging from a subway station. Seconds later, she stabbed the 32-year-old woman, also in the abdomen.Both victims were taken to hospital. Police have not identified them as authorities continue to notify their relatives.“This was an extraordinarily dangerous situation unfolding in the heart of Times Square, the crossroads of the world,” Tisch said.NYC mayor Zohran Mamdani and Tisch praised the officers who confronted the woman, saying their actions helped prevent the situation from escalating further in one of the city's busiest tourist areas.“We know that those families’ lives have been shattered by what took place today, and we will continue to hold them close as the hours and days and weeks continue from this moment," Mamdani said.Police temporarily shut part of 7th Avenue and urged the public to stay away from the area as investigators examined the scene.The incident came as violent crime continues to decline across New York City. Homicides are down 24% so far this year and are on course to potentially reach their lowest level in decades.It was, however, the second fatal stabbing in Times Square this year. A man was killed in a stabbing in the same area in May.
Article Summary: The 49-year-old Queens woman was confronted by NYPD officers shortly after stabbing a 32- year-old woman and a 68-year old man on Monday afternoon. The younger woman died from her injuries, while the man remained in stable condition. The dramatic confrontation unfolded near an NYPD substation outside One Times Square, where officers spent several minutes attempting to persuade the woman to put down the weapons.

Article Title: US states, consumer watchdog file lawsuit against Amazon for manipulating advertising prices
Article Text:
The company's shares reportedly fell 2.5 per cent after the lawsuit was announced.

US consumer watchdog, Federal Trade Commission (FTC), and a group of 22 US states filed a lawsuit against Amazon on Monday, accusing the company of overcharging its advertising customers by manipulating the online auctions that set ad prices.The company's shares reportedly fell 2.5 per cent after the lawsuit was announced.Amazon has gained nearly $20 billion from over a million advertising customers since 2019, the FTC and states allege in the lawsuit.According to a filed complaint reported by the BBC, "Amazon overrides and replaces the actual auction results with higher prices set by Amazon to increase its profits.""Consumers are suffering, have suffered, and will continue to suffer substantial injury as a result", it said."The FTC wants the public to believe this case is about higher prices for consumers. It is not," Amazon said in its statement.In a statement to the BBC, the company said it "strongly disagrees" with the premise of the lawsuit and called it "misguided".The FTC and the states also alleged that Amazon's practices have harmed consumers, as the additional advertising costs are ultimately passed on to shoppers.On Amazon's e-commerce platform, brands and sellers compete to place Sponsored Product and Sponsored Brands ads when consumers search for products using keywords.These ad placements are then auctioned to the highest bidder.The complaint alleges that Amazon secretly charged advertisers more through so-called "second price" auctions. Under this system, advertisers expect to pay one cent more than the next-highest bidder for each auction they win.However, the complaint alleges that Amazon charged Sponsored Products advertisers their own winning bid nearly 80 per cent of the time.The lawsuit said Amazon's practices were driven by its dissatisfaction with the revenue generated through its advertising auctions.Amazon said the FTC "fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate"."Advertisers adjust bids based on real-world performance, not descriptions of auction mechanics," the company said.Amazon added that average winning bids fell 50 per cent between 2019 and 2025 for Sponsored Products search ads. It also said roughly 92 per cent of placed ads are not awarded to the highest bidder.Notably, Amazon has faced legal action from the FTC in the past.Last year, the company settled a case brought by the FTC, which alleged that it had enrolled millions of consumers in its Prime subscription service without their consent and knowingly made it difficult for them to cancel.Amazon agreed to pay $2.5 billion to settle the case, including civil penalties and refunds to consumers.
Article Summary: US consumer watchdog, Federal Trade Commission (FTC), and a group of 22 US states filed a lawsuit against Amazon on Monday. The company's shares reportedly fell 2.5 per cent after the lawsuit was announced. Amazon has gained nearly $20 billion from over a million advertising customers since 2019, the FTC and states allege in the lawsuit.

Article Title: Oklahoma man found beneath a flyover at 92 pounds after 20 years of addiction goes from homelessness to graduating with a 4.0 GPA and two degrees
Article Text:
Addiction left him homeless and weighing just 92 pounds

Officers found him beneath an I-40 overpass

Recovery gave him a chance to rebuild his life

He went back to college and earned a 4.0 GPA

From homelessness to helping others find hope

Danny Ellerd’s life once appeared to be heading towards an early death. After years of addiction and homelessness, he was found beneath an I-40 overpass in Oklahoma City weighing just 92 pounds, according to recovery organisation Hope Is Alive. Officers initially planned to book him on outstanding warrants, but his physical condition was so severe that he was taken to hospital instead. Doctors worked to save his life and his hand, which had been badly affected by an infection linked to intravenous heroin use. What followed was a dramatic turnaround. Ellerd entered recovery, rebuilt his life and eventually returned to education. He went on to study at Oklahoma State University-Oklahoma City, where he earned two associate degrees and maintained a perfect 4.0 GPA. His transformation later extended beyond his own recovery, as he began working with and supporting people experiencing homelessness and addiction.Ellerd’s descent into addiction lasted for years and eventually left him homeless in Oklahoma City. Hope Is Alive says he spent 15 years in addiction, endured years of homelessness and experienced multiple overdoses. Other accounts connected to Oklahoma State University have described his period of active addiction as lasting nearly 20 years.During those years, Ellerd lived in abandoned houses and tents and eventually found himself without a stable home. His addiction had taken such a heavy toll that his family feared for his survival. At one point, his father reportedly saw people holding signs on Oklahoma City streets before realising that one of them was his own son. Ellerd later described his life during addiction as one marked by hopelessness and a belief that he had no way out. His circumstances would soon reach an even more dangerous point when officers encountered him beneath an I-40 overpass.The encounter with police became a critical turning point in Ellerd’s life. According to Hope Is Alive, officers found him beneath an I-40 overpass and he weighed just 92 pounds. They initially intended to deal with outstanding warrants, but his physical condition was so poor that he was taken to an emergency room instead. Doctors treated him for serious health problems and worked to save his hand, which had developed a severe infection associated with intravenous heroin use. An Oklahoma State University-linked account gives his weight as 90 pounds rather than 92, making the precise figure slightly inconsistent across accounts, but both sources agree that he was dangerously underweight and in extremely poor health. Hope Is Alive says Ellerd eventually entered its recovery programme directly from hospital, carrying little more than a Walmart bag of clothes. What began as a medical emergency ultimately became the starting point for a radically different chapter of his life.Leaving the hospital was only the beginning of Ellerd’s recovery. He entered a structured recovery programme through Hope Is Alive and began working to rebuild the stability that addiction had taken from him. The organisation says recovery gave him structure, accountability and support as he worked to establish a new life. His transformation also became increasingly connected to helping others facing similar circumstances. He became involved in recovery support and eventually worked with organisations serving people experiencing homelessness. Oklahoma State University later highlighted his commitment to service, noting that his own experiences with addiction and homelessness had shaped his desire to empower others. By the time he was studying at OSU-OKC, Ellerd was balancing education with work and service. He was working as a Shelter Advocate for City Care, supporting people experiencing homelessness, while also volunteering with Hope Is Alive Ministries and sponsoring men in recovery. His past had become a source of motivation to help people who were still struggling.Education became another major part of Ellerd’s transformation. He enrolled at Oklahoma State University-Oklahoma City and studied Computer Information Systems while managing work and other responsibilities. In 2023, he was selected for Cohort 4 of OSU-OKC’s Center for Social Innovation. At the time, accounts from the centre described him as simultaneously working part-time, managing a recovery home and attending college full-time. Despite those demands, he maintained a 4.0 GPA. The university later recognised Ellerd as a 2025 Women for OSU Scholar, citing his academic performance, leadership and community involvement. He participated in the President’s Leadership Class, the Things That Matter Club and Phi Theta Kappa. His academic achievements culminated in two associate degrees. Ellerd earned an Associate in Applied Science in Computer Information Systems and an Associate in Science in Enterprise Development, completing his studies with a perfect 4.0 GPA.Ellerd’s transformation did not end with his graduation. His experiences with addiction and homelessness became central to his efforts to support others going through similar struggles. He worked as a Shelter Advocate for City Care and remained involved in recovery support, helping people who were facing circumstances similar to those he had once endured. He also turned his experience into a book titled Recovery Is Possible: The Story of My Journey Through Addiction and Into Recovery. He later launched a campaign aimed at distributing 1,000 copies of the book free to homeless people and people struggling with addiction who could not afford it. His journey therefore came full circle. The man who was once found beneath an Oklahoma City overpass weighing just 92 pounds had gone on to rebuild his life, return to college, graduate with two degrees and a 4.0 GPA, and dedicate part of his life to helping others find a way out of homelessness and addiction.

Article Title: A Guatemalan immigrant began delivering pizzas in Dallas in 1987; decades later she built a franchise training organisation
Article Text:
Representative Image of a leading figure in the franchise pathway illustrating progressive learning and business development (AI-generated image)

Why Aicha Bascaro says franchisors teach the brand but not the business

How the academy's three programs serve different levels of a franchise organisation

What Bascaro built beyond the academy's formal programs

What comes next for the American Franchise Academy after 10 years

Aicha Bascaro arrived in the United States as an immigrant from Guatemala and, in 1987, took a job delivering pizzas at a Domino's restaurant in Dallas, Texas. What began as an entry-level job became the starting point for a career spanning more than three decades and almost every level of the franchise industry. Bascaro worked as a crew member and manager before moving into senior positions, including director of operations, vice president, international consultant and eventually brand president, where she oversaw more than 300 locations across the country. Along the way, she saw a gap that she believed was easy to overlook: franchise owners could be taught how to operate a particular brand without necessarily receiving the broader business education needed to lead and grow a company. That idea eventually became the foundation for the American Franchise Academy. In 2016, a struggling franchisee contacted Bascaro looking for help with a failing business, and instead of simply offering informal advice, she developed a structured training program around the problems he was facing. The American Franchise Academy was founded on July 18, 2016, and a decade later has grown into a specialised organisation focused on business management education for franchisees and their teams.According to the International Franchise Association, Bascaro created the academy around what she considers one of the franchise industry's biggest gaps. Franchisors generally provide extensive training on their own brands, teaching new owners how their particular systems work and how to operate according to established standards. Bascaro's view is that this brand-specific training does not necessarily cover the wider business skills required to lead and grow a franchise. She has described the distinction simply: franchisors provide the brand and train franchisees to operate it, but they cannot provide the broader business acumen. That, she says, is where the American Franchise Academy comes in, offering training focused on helping franchisees become stronger business leaders rather than simply better operators of a particular brand.The idea came from Bascaro's own experience in the industry. Having progressed from delivering pizzas to senior leadership roles, she had spent years seeing how responsibilities changed as people moved from working inside individual locations to managing larger operations. By the time the struggling franchisee contacted her in 2016, she had accumulated the practical experience to recognise that his problem was not necessarily a lack of effort or knowledge about the brand itself. He needed a more structured understanding of how to manage the business. That first training program eventually became the starting point for an academy built around a much broader idea: franchise ownership requires more than knowing the rules of the brand.The American Franchise Academy now divides its main curriculum into three programs designed for different levels of responsibility within a franchise organisation.MANAGE provides business-management education for single-unit franchisees and unit managers. The program is aimed at people responsible for the performance of an individual location and focuses on giving them a structured foundation in franchise business management.LEAD is designed for district managers, who oversee multiple locations and therefore operate at a different level from managers responsible for a single unit. The academy offers certification through the program, reflecting the additional responsibilities involved in managing teams and operations across several locations.At the top of the academy's structure is COMMAND, its flagship program. It brings together the broader curriculum intended for franchisees who want to lead and grow their businesses. The three-level structure allows the academy to address people at different stages of the franchise hierarchy rather than treating every operator as though they face the same challenges.Over its first decade, the academy says it has certified more than 400 district managers, more than 200 unit managers and around 100 franchisees. Its participants have come from some of the biggest names in franchising, including McDonald's, Popeyes, Dairy Queen, Subway, Dunkin' and Anytime Fitness. Those numbers also illustrate how the academy has moved beyond the single franchisee whose problems inspired Bascaro to create the original training program. What began as an attempt to help one struggling business has developed into a formal education system serving franchise professionals across multiple major brands.Bascaro's work has expanded beyond classroom-style certification. During the academy's first decade, she also built a wider collection of educational material around franchise management, including three Amazon bestselling books and a weekly blog focused on franchising and business education. She also hosts the Franchise Success Formulas podcast, which has attracted more than 19,000 YouTube subscribers. Together, the books, blog, podcast and certification programs have allowed the academy to reach people at different stages of their franchise careers and through different formats.Bascaro has also received recognition within the franchise industry. Her honours include being named to Nation's Restaurant News' 2022 Power List and receiving a Trailblazer Award. She also serves as a Certified Franchise Executive instructor for the International Franchise Association. The broader body of work reflects the same distinction that shaped the academy from the beginning. Bascaro's focus is not simply on teaching franchisees how to follow the operating model of a particular company. Instead, the academy treats business management as a separate area of education that franchise operators can continue developing throughout their careers. That distinction becomes particularly important when a franchisee grows. Running one location and leading a larger franchise operation involve different levels of responsibility, and the academy's programs are structured around those different stages.The academy is now looking beyond its first decade and toward expanding the reach of its training. One of its priorities is developing multilingual programs that could make the academy's business-management education available to franchise operators around the world rather than primarily serving English-speaking participants. The organisation is also expanding its work directly with franchisors. Through its franchisor partnership strategy, the academy aims to help individual brands provide structured business-management education to their franchise networks through an outside training organisation. Instead of requiring franchisees to find this kind of education independently, the model would allow brands to make it part of the wider support available to their operators.
Article Summary: Aicha Bascaro is the founder of the American Franchise Academy. She believes franchisors teach the brand but not the business skills needed to lead and grow a company. The academy offers three programs designed for different levels of responsibility within a franchise organisation.

Article Title: In 1941, comedian Jack Oakie bought a California ranch; decades later his widow fought to save its last 9 acres from development
Article Text:
Jack Oakie, PC: Wikipedia

Why Victoria Oakie fought to protect Oakridge

How the estate survived residential development

What remains of Marwyck Ranch and Oakridge today

Why Oakridge matters beyond Barbara Stanwyck and Jack Oakie

In 1937, actress Barbara Stanwyck built a roughly 6,000-square-foot residence on a hilltop in Northridge, in Los Angeles' San Fernando Valley. The house was part of Marwyck Ranch, a roughly 130-acre thoroughbred breeding and training operation associated with Stanwyck and her business partner and agent, Zeppo Marx. The home's architectural history is disputed: it has traditionally been attributed to architect Paul R. Williams, although Robert Finkelhor is listed as the architect of record on the original building permit. Stanwyck lived at the property for about two years before marrying actor Robert Taylor and moving closer to Hollywood. In 1941, comedian Jack Oakie purchased the estate and renamed it Oakridge, eventually making it his longtime home with actress Victoria Horne. Oakie, best known for playing Benzino Napaloni in Charlie Chaplin's The Great Dictator, maintained a citrus orchard and Afghan Hounds on the grounds. After his death in 1978, Victoria continued efforts to preserve the property. Oakridge was designated a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument in 1990, and she donated it to the University of Southern California in 2000. When residential development later threatened the surviving estate, the City of Los Angeles acquired its remaining 9.47 acres in 2009.Stanwyck lived at the Northridge property from 1937 to 1939. After marrying Robert Taylor in 1939, she and Taylor moved closer to the Hollywood film community, and Stanwyck eventually sold the estate. In 1941, Oakie acquired the property and renamed it Oakridge. He initially lived there with his first wife, actress Venita Vardon. Their marriage ended in divorce in 1944, and Vardon died in a 1948 plane crash. Oakie married actress Victoria Horne in 1950, and the couple continued to make Oakridge their home. Oakie maintained a citrus orchard on the property and kept Afghan Hounds, reportedly having as many as 100 dogs on the grounds at one point. When Oakie died in 1978, Victoria remained at Oakridge for another 25 years and became closely associated with efforts to preserve the estate as the San Fernando Valley around it underwent rapid development.Oakridge was designated Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 484 in 1990, giving the property formal historic recognition as development continued to transform the Valley's former ranches, agricultural land and large estates. In 2000, Victoria donated Oakridge to the University of Southern California's School of Cinematic Arts. Her instructions called for USC to sell the estate and use the proceeds to establish a university chair in comedy named for Jack Oakie. Victoria died in 2003 at the age of 91, 25 years after her husband. Her donation gave the property a future beyond her lifetime, but it did not immediately guarantee that the surrounding acreage would remain undeveloped.After USC took ownership, developers proposed residential construction on the remaining property. One proposal called for 28 single-family homes on land surrounding the historic house, a plan that would have significantly changed the open setting around the residence. The development effort ultimately failed when the deal fell out of escrow amid the economic downturn of the late 2000s. The property's future remained uncertain until Los Angeles officials became involved in efforts to preserve it through public ownership.Los Angeles City Councilmember Greig Smith played a role in efforts to secure Oakridge for the city. In 2009, the City of Los Angeles acquired the property for $3.35 million using Quimby and related park fees. City records indicate that approximately $3.8 million in Quimby funds had been secured for the acquisition, rehabilitation and improvement of the estate. The purchase transferred Oakridge into public ownership, with the property dedicated as parkland in perpetuity. Instead of being converted into the proposed residential development, the historic house and the remaining acreage were preserved as part of the city's park system.Very little of the original Marwyck Ranch survives. Sources vary on the precise size of the original property, with historical accounts putting it at roughly 127 to 130 acres, while numerous accounts of Oakridge describe the original ranch as approximately 130 acres. The surviving Oakridge property covers 9.47 acres. The historic residence remains the centrepiece of the site, although its architectural attribution requires qualification. Paul R. Williams has traditionally been associated with the design and is frequently credited as its architect, but Robert Finkelhor is identified as the architect of record on the original 1937 building permit. The house remains an important surviving example of the large country residences that once appeared across the San Fernando Valley.The landscape around Oakridge has changed dramatically since Stanwyck established the estate. In the 1930s and 1940s, Northridge and surrounding parts of the Valley were substantially more rural, with agricultural land, citrus groves, horse ranches and large country properties. Hollywood figures were drawn to the area because it offered space and privacy while remaining within reach of the city's film studios. Pat LoPresti, who served as outreach committee chair for the Oakridge Estate Park Advisory Board, has discussed Oakridge in the context of this earlier San Fernando Valley, recalling a period when citrus groves and Hollywood figures were part of Northridge's landscape.Oakridge's significance extends beyond the famous people who lived there. The property's history connects several stages in the transformation of the San Fernando Valley, from its agricultural and equestrian past to its association with Hollywood and, eventually, the suburban development that replaced many of its ranches and estates. Stanwyck's residence became part of the Marwyck thoroughbred operation before becoming Jack Oakie's home, while Victoria Horne Oakie later became central to efforts to preserve the property. Her work helped secure its historic designation, and her 2000 donation to USC provided another chapter in the effort to determine the estate's future. When residential development subsequently threatened the remaining property, the City of Los Angeles acquired Oakridge in 2009.The original Marwyck Ranch is gone, but a 9.47-acre portion survives as Oakridge. The property cannot recreate the landscape that once surrounded Stanwyck and Oakie, but its historic house and grounds preserve a tangible piece of the earlier San Fernando Valley. What remains is a small fragment of a much larger ranch, offering a physical link to a period when citrus groves, horse properties and Hollywood estates occupied land that is now surrounded by a densely developed Los Angeles.
Article Summary: Actress Barbara Stanwyck built a roughly 6,000-square-foot residence on a hilltop in Northridge, in Los Angeles' San Fernando Valley. In 1941, comedian Jack Oakie purchased the estate and renamed it Oakridge. Oakie, best known for playing Benzino Napaloni in Charlie Chaplin's The Great Dictator, maintained a citrus orchard and Afghan Hounds on the grounds. Oakridge was designated a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument in 1990.

Article Title: Times Square stabbing: 1 killed, another critically injured; suspect shot dead by NYPD
Article Text:
1 dead, 1 critically injured in Times Square stabbing; police kill suspect

At least one person was killed and another critically injured after a woman allegedly stabbed two people in New York City's Times Square before she was fatally shot by police, authorities said.The stabbings occurred at around 42nd Street and Seventh Avenue on Monday, according to police. The suspect, described by authorities as apparently emotionally disturbed, fled north toward an NYPD substation, where officers confronted her.Police said the woman was armed with two large knives when officers encountered her. Bystander video showed several officers surrounding the woman, with at least one appearing to use a taser before she moved toward officers while brandishing the knives. Officers then opened fire.The suspect was taken to a hospital, where she died from her injuries, according to police sources.One of the stabbing victims, a woman, also died at a hospital, police said. The second victim suffered life-threatening injuries.Police officials stressed that the incident does not appear to be terror-related and that the suspect appeared to be emotionally disturbed.The shooting took place near an NYPD substation just outside One Times Square, one of New York City's most heavily policed and visited areas.Police cordoned off the area and closed part of Seventh Avenue as officers investigated the incident. Authorities have urged the public to stay away from the area.
Article Summary: The suspect, described by authorities as apparently emotionally disturbed, fled north toward an NYPD substation, where officers confronted her. Police said the woman was armed with two large knives when officers encountered her. Bystander video showed several officers surrounding the woman, with at least one appearing to use a taser before she moved toward officers while brandishing the knives. Officers then opened fire.

Article Title: Lahore inflation squeezes household budgets as food, rent and utility costs rise
Article Text:
People walk through a market to shop for grocery and other items

Vegetable, LPG prices add to public anger

Rising inflation in Pakistan's Lahore has intensified financial pressures on ordinary citizens, with soaring prices of food, rent, utilities and other essentials making it increasingly difficult for low-income families to make ends meet, new agency ANI reported.Residents said the rising cost of basic commodities has made it difficult for some households to afford even two meals a day. Prices of flour, cooking oil, pulses, vegetables and other necessities have continued to rise, while daily-wage workers and low-income earners said their incomes have failed to keep pace with inflation.Citizens also raised concerns over sharply higher vegetable prices, saying commonly consumed items such as potatoes and tomatoes have become increasingly unaffordable. Residents said vegetables were being sold for around Rs 150 to Rs 300 per kilogram, depending on the item and market.One resident appealed to the government to address the difficulties faced by poor families, saying rising food prices, rent and utility bills had made household management extremely challenging. Families on limited incomes, he said, were increasingly being forced to choose between food, rent, medicines and other essential expenses.ANI reports that people living on modest pensions were struggling to manage household expenses, particularly when they also had children, medical costs and other financial responsibilities.Residents also criticised the government over LPG prices, alleging that the fuel was being sold above official rates in some markets. They questioned who would regulate traders and ensure enforcement of government price controls.Rickshaw driver Usman Ali said rising fuel and essential commodity prices had severely affected his livelihood, leaving little or nothing to save after meeting basic household expenses.Citizens further questioned why lower petrol prices had not resulted in cheaper food and other essential commodities, asking why reductions in fuel costs were not being reflected in market prices.
Article Summary: Rising prices of food, rent, utilities and other essentials making it increasingly difficult for low-income families to make ends meet. Prices of flour, cooking oil, pulses, vegetables and other necessities have continued to rise. Citizens also raised concerns over sharply higher vegetable prices. Residents also criticised the government over LPG prices.

Article Title: Kabul, Kashmir, Mumbai, Pahalgam: Hafiz Saeed’s deadly four-decade terror trail
Article Text:
Four decades of Lashkar: How Hafiz Saeed’s network moved from Afghanistan to Kashmir (Associated press image)

LeT's major attacks

The Afghan war that created LeT's foundations

Deadly Embrace: Pakistan, America, and the Future of the Global Jihad

Why Lashkar-e-Taiba was established

From Kunar to Kashmir

Lashkar-e-Taiba: From 9/11 to Mumbai

Who is Hafiz Saeed

Hafiz Saeed - From cleric to terrorist

LeT survives Pakistani ban after 9/11

Four decades of evolution

From Kashmir insurgency to Mumbai

Why Afghanistan remained part of the network

Saeed's legal history and the Pahalgam case

From Afghan jihad to Kashmir

From Afghan jihad to Pahalgam

The legal case against Lashkar-e-Taiba founder Hafiz Muhammad Saeed has acquired a fresh dimension in India.
