In July 2026, the National Investigation Agency named Saeed in a supplementary chargesheet in the Pahalgam terror attack case, charging him in his individual capacity and as the founder and chief of Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) and its active proxy, The Resistance Front (TRF). The NIA mentioned a cross-border conspiracy behind the April 22, 2025 attack, which killed 26 civilians. A special NIA court subsequently issued a non-bailable warrant against Saeed.The development came as Mumbai Police separately began proceedings for a trial in absentia against Saeed and five other Pakistan-based accused in the 2008 Mumbai terror attacks. The proclamation covers Saeed, LeT operations chief Zaki-ur-Rehman Lakhvi, Sajid Mir, Abu Alqama, Asim alias Abu Qahafa and Major Abdur Rehman Pasha. The police have also approached the Union home ministry to facilitate service of the proclamation orders through Interpol.The two cases, separated by 17 years, bring together different phases of LeT's history. One concerns an attack in Kashmir, the region that became the organisation's principal battlefield in the 1990s. The other concerns the Mumbai attacks, which demonstrated how far LeT's operational reach had expanded beyond the Kashmir insurgency.But LeT did not begin in Kashmir, nor did Hafiz Saeed first emerge as a militant leader there. The organisation's institutional roots can be traced to the Afghan jihad of the 1980s, when Pakistan became a major centre for the mobilisation, training and movement of Islamist fighters.The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 created an environment in which Islamist networks from Pakistan and other parts of the Muslim world expanded rapidly. Among the prominent figures associated with this mobilisation was Palestinian scholar Abdullah Azzam, who helped organise foreign volunteers for the Afghan jihad and promoted the idea of jihad as a broader obligation extending beyond a single battlefield.It was in this environment that Azzam worked with Hafiz Saeed, a Pakistani Sunni scholar who had studied in Saudi Arabia. According to Bruce Riedel's, the two were involved in establishing Markaz-ud-Dawa-wal-Irshad (MDI), a religious organisation that combined missionary activity with support for jihad. MDI developed training infrastructure in Afghanistan, including in Kunar province, where recruits could gain battlefield experience. Riedel also records links between the organisation and Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI).Lashkar-e-Taiba subsequently emerged as the military wing associated with this network. The US state department describes LeT as having formed in the late 1980s as the militant wing of MDI, an organisation originally established in opposition to the Soviet presence in Afghanistan. The Australian government dates LeT's formation as a military organisation to 1989.The exact formation date therefore varies depending on whether the establishment of MDI, the creation of its military wing or the later formalisation of LeT is being referred to. What is clearer is the sequence: the Afghan jihad provided the organisation's early ideological, human and training infrastructure, while the end of the Soviet war opened the way for that infrastructure to be redirected towards other conflicts.LeT's early purpose was shaped by two connected objectives: participation in the Afghan jihad and preparation for jihad in Kashmir and India. Riedel describes MDI's objective as applying the experience of the Afghan war to Kashmir and India, including training Kashmiris alongside Afghan mujahideen so they could gain combat experience.The changing situation in Afghanistan accelerated that transition. The Soviet withdrawal meant that the battlefield that had brought together thousands of militants was no longer the same. At the same time, violence in Jammu and Kashmir was rising sharply.The Australian government's account of LeT's history says the organisation was originally formed to wage militant jihad against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan and shifted its focus to the insurgency in Indian-administered Kashmir during the 1990s after Soviet troops withdrew. It identifies the organisation's stated objective as uniting Kashmir with Pakistan, while noting that its broader ideological objectives extended beyond Kashmir.Kashmir thus became the next major theatre in which the organisation could deploy the personnel, training and networks developed during the Afghan war.The shift towards Kashmir coincided with the rapid growth of the insurgency there. Riedel records that incidents of violence in Kashmir rose from 390 in 1988 to 2,100 in 1989 and nearly 4,000 in 1990. Against this backdrop, Saeed's organisation began establishing infrastructure in and around Kashmir while maintaining training facilities in Pakistan and Afghanistan.LeT's emergence also coincided with changes among the various groups fighting in Kashmir. The Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front advocated an independent Kashmir, while Pakistan's security establishment increasingly favoured groups committed to the territory's integration with Pakistan. Riedel describes efforts to strengthen pro-Pakistan organisations and isolate the JKLF, which was regarded as too independent. Hizbul Mujahideen became a major pro-Pakistan militant force, while LeT developed its own network and capabilities.By the 1990s, Kashmir had become LeT's principal operational theatre. The organisation developed training and recruitment networks and directed fighters towards attacks on Indian security forces. Stephen Tankel, in, describes Kashmir as the group's primary objective even as its connections to the wider global jihadist movement expanded.This distinction is important. LeT developed relationships with al Qaida and other jihadist groups, but its core focus remained India and Kashmir. Riedel similarly distinguishes between the different objectives of the groups operating in the region, noting that the Afghan Taliban remained primarily focused on Afghanistan while LeT concentrated on South Asia. At the operational level, however, their cooperation increased.Saeed's prominence grew alongside the institutional development of MDI and LeT. He was not simply the leader of an armed organisation. The network around him combined religious propagation, education, charity and terror activity.Riedel describes Saeed as a prominent Pakistani Sunni scholar who worked with Azzam in developing MDI. The organisation's combination of religious activity and military infrastructure provided the foundation for the later growth of LeT.LeT's recruitment base was also closely connected to Pakistani society. Riedel writes that the organisation was predominantly Punjabi and recruited from many of the same communities and neighbourhoods as the Pakistani army and ISI. He also describes LeT camps located near army bases and the involvement of retired military personnel in training fighters.The nature and extent of state support for LeT has remained a matter of dispute, but the organisation's relationship with Pakistan's security establishment became an important part of its history. The United Nations Security Council identifies LeT as a Pakistan-based organisation and records its links with al Qaida and the Taliban, as well as its use of Jamaat-ud-Dawa for financial, logistical and infrastructural support.The September 11, 2001 attacks changed the environment for militant organisations operating from Pakistan. The United States designated LeT as a Foreign Terrorist Organisation in December 2001, while Pakistan banned the group in January 2002.The ban, however, did not eliminate the network. The US state department says Saeed subsequently changed the group's name to Jamaat-ud-Dawa and expanded its humanitarian activities, while continuing to disseminate its message through JuD's media outlets.Riedel similarly writes that although LeT was formally banned, it continued to operate and Saeed remained in charge. He describes the organisation's large facility at Muridke near Lahore, which included schools, dormitories, a garment factory, an iron foundry and a mosque.This structure helped the network maintain a presence beyond its armed operations. Religious institutions, charitable activity, fundraising and recruitment provided a broader organisational base that could continue even when the LeT name itself faced restrictions.The United Nations says LeT used JuD as a front through which it provided financial, logistical and infrastructural support for terrorist activity. It also records that an al Qaida operative, Abu Zubaydah, was captured in 2002 in a LeT safe house in Faisalabad, illustrating the organisation's connections to the wider jihadist network.The years after 2001 saw LeT's operational reach extend beyond the traditional Kashmir battlefield. The United Nations records that the organisation conducted terrorist operations against military and civilian targets from the 1990s onwards, including attacks in New Delhi and Mumbai and the December 2001 Parliament attack, in which Jaish-e-Mohammed was also involved.The 2008 Mumbai attacks represented the most significant expansion of that reach. Ten attackers carried out coordinated assaults across Mumbai between November 26 and 29, killing 166 people. The attack targeted several locations, including the Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, the Oberoi-Trident and Nariman House.The operation also demonstrated the organisational depth behind LeT's attacks. Riedel's account details the role of David Coleman Headley, who joined LeT in Pakistan and later conducted reconnaissance in Mumbai. Between 2005 and 2008, Headley travelled repeatedly to India, studying targets, recording locations and reporting back to LeT.The Mumbai operation therefore represented more than an extension of the Kashmir insurgency. It demonstrated the organisation's ability to plan and execute a complex attack far from its traditional theatre while drawing on personnel, training and logistical networks developed over decades.The shift to Kashmir did not end LeT's involvement in Afghanistan. Instead, the two theatres became connected through overlapping militant networks.Riedel wrote that LeT became increasingly active in Afghanistan, including operations against Indian interests and clashes with Nato forces. He also described growing operational links between LeT and the Afghan Taliban, particularly the Haqqani network.The United Nations likewise records LeT's activity in Afghanistan and its links with al Qaida and the Taliban. The Australian government has documented LeT's continued presence in Afghanistan and reported that the UN estimated the group had close to 1,000 members operating there in May 2020.Afghanistan therefore remained an important part of LeT's network even after Kashmir became its main operational focus. The relationships, training environments and infrastructure developed during the Afghan jihad continued to provide connections to other militant organisations.Saeed's subsequent legal history illustrates the difference between Pakistan's formal action against LeT and the organisation's continued existence through associated structures.Pakistan arrested Saeed in 2019 on terrorism-financing charges. He was convicted in several cases and received additional sentences in subsequent proceedings. The UN Security Council's current sanctions information says Saeed is in Pakistani custody serving a cumulative 78-year sentence following convictions in seven terrorism-financing cases.India, meanwhile, has continued to pursue him over alleged involvement in major terror attacks attributed to LeT.The latest development is the NIA's supplementary chargesheet in the Pahalgam case. The agency has named Saeed both individually and as the chief of LeT and TRF, alleging that he was part of the wider conspiracy behind the April 2025 attack.The subsequent non-bailable warrant followed the NIA's request for Saeed's arrest and custodial interrogation. Meanwhile, Mumbai Police has begun the process for an in-absentia trial against Saeed and five other Pakistan-based accused in the 26/11 case.Lashkar-e-Taiba's four-decade history can be traced through a sequence of changing battlefields and organisational forms. Its foundations were laid during the Afghan jihad, when Hafiz Saeed and Abdullah Azzam helped build MDI and the networks around it. After the Soviet withdrawal, the organisation redirected much of its experience and infrastructure towards Kashmir, where it became a major Pakistan-based militant group.The 2002 ban did not erase the network. It adapted through Jamaat-ud-Dawa and other associated structures, while maintaining religious, charitable and recruitment networks across Pakistan. Its links with militant groups operating in Afghanistan also survived, even as India and Kashmir remained its central focus.The Mumbai attacks showed how far that network could project violence beyond Kashmir. The Pahalgam investigation has now brought the story back to the same region where LeT established much of its early operational identity.The latest legal proceedings against Saeed therefore sit at the end of a history that began not in Mumbai or Pahalgam, but in the Afghan jihad of the 1980s.
Article Summary: The legal case against Hafiz Muhammad Saeed has acquired a fresh dimension in India. The National Investigation Agency named Saeed in a supplementary chargesheet in the Pahalgam terror attack case. The development came as Mumbai Police separately began proceedings for a trial in absentia against Saeed and five other Pakistan-based accused in the 2008 Mumbai attacks.

Article Title: Pakistan hospital fire: 8 officials suspended over deaths of 14 newborns
Article Text: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered the suspension of eight officials and directed that criminal proceedings be initiated against those found responsible for a fire that killed 14 newborns at a hospital in Islamabad, his office said on Saturday.Sharif issued the orders after an interim report by an investigative committee found serious lapses in fire safety and emergency preparedness at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS).The fire broke out on the third-floor nursery on Wednesday, where 15 newborns were being treated. The blaze spread rapidly, and hospital staff were able to rescue only one baby, officials said.The committee found that the nursery had neither a fire alarm nor a sprinkler system. It also said the hospital lacked detailed procedures and adequate training to deal with fires and other emergencies.The report said supervisory staff were not present when the fire broke out. Two nurses, a female security guard and a house officer were in the ward at the time.Emergency services were alerted six minutes after the fire started, while the first responders arrived 15 minutes after receiving the call, according to the interim report.Investigators also found that only two of the hospital's 13 standard operating procedures dealt with fires or other emergencies.“Those guilty of criminal negligence deserve no leniency,” Sharif was quoted as saying by the Associated Press. He ordered departmental and criminal proceedings against officials identified by the inquiry committee.Those facing action include the hospital's executive director, two joint executive directors, the head of the neonatal department, two doctors, the assistant director for security and the head of the Capital Development Authority's emergency services.Sharif also approved action against the private company responsible for hospital security and its officials.The government has announced compensation of 5 million Pakistani rupees (around $18,000) for each bereaved family.The interim report also recommended recognition for a nurse who risked her life to save a newborn before the flames spread through the ward. Sharif approved the recommendation to confer the Sitara-i-Khidmat, a state award for public service, on her.The deaths have triggered public anger and demands for accountability from grieving families and civil society groups.The incident has also prompted wider reviews of fire-safety arrangements at hospitals across Pakistan. Punjab authorities this week ordered an immediate assessment of fire-safety systems, firefighting equipment and emergency-response facilities at hospitals across the province.The fire was among Pakistan's deadliest recent tragedies involving children. In June, 14 schoolchildren were killed when the roof of an under-construction tutoring centre collapsed in Lahore.
Article Summary: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered the suspension of eight officials. He has also directed that criminal proceedings be initiated against those found responsible for a fire that killed 14 newborns at a hospital in Islamabad. The fire broke out on the third-floor nursery on Wednesday, where 15 newborns were being treated.

Article Title: Pakistan: Three missing men found dead with alleged torture marks in Balochistan
Article Text:
Representative file photo (IANS photo)

Three bodies recovered in Balochistan's Usta Muhammad have reportedly been identified as men who had earlier gone missing, with local sources alleging that they were forcibly disappeared after being detained by Pakistani security forces.According to The Balochistan Post, the deceased have been identified as Hafiz Mohammad Waqas, a Levies personnel from Machh in Bolan, his brother Mittha Khan, son of Nawab Khan, and Maqbool Ahmed, son of Jan Mohammad, a resident of Dasht Sabzband.Waqas was reportedly taken into custody and forcibly disappeared in May 2026. The three bodies were recovered from Usta Muhammad on August 24, according to local sources cited by the publication.The sources said the bodies bore apparent signs of torture. However, the circumstances surrounding their deaths have not been independently established, and no official findings from an investigation have been made public.The recoveries come amid reports of more than 15 bodies being found in different parts of Balochistan in recent days, including Panjgur, Mastung and Kharan. Several bodies recovered from Panjgur were allegedly identified as people who had previously been reported missing, while the identities of others remain unknown.The latest cases have renewed scrutiny of allegations of enforced disappearances in Balochistan, where rights groups and political organisations have for years raised concerns over the fate of missing people.Baloch political and human rights organisations have accused Pakistani security institutions of detaining people and, in some cases, killing them in custody before abandoning their bodies. Pakistan's authorities and security institutions have repeatedly denied involvement in enforced disappearances and allegations of extrajudicial killings.Rights groups and political organisations have called for credible and transparent investigations into the reported disappearances and deaths. They have also demanded that missing individuals be produced before courts, their families be informed of their whereabouts, and anyone accused of wrongdoing be subjected to due legal process.
Article Summary: Three bodies recovered in Balochistan's Usta Muhammad have reportedly been identified as men who had earlier gone missing. Local sources allege they were forcibly disappeared after being detained by Pakistani security forces. The circumstances surrounding their deaths have not been independently established, and no official findings from an investigation have been made public.

Article Title: 15 newborns killed in fire at Islamabad hospital's gynaecology ward in Pakistan
Article Text:
The fire reportedly started after an air-conditioner compressor exploded inside the nursery, according to rescue sources.

Poll Vote & Share your view What should hospitals prioritise to prevent fire-related tragedies? Stronger fire-safety measures Regular safety inspections 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

15 newborns died after a fire broke out in the gynaecology ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad on Wednesday.According to PIMS officials, the nursery housed 16 newborns when the fire broke out, with only one baby rescued from the ward, reported local outlet Geo News. The fire reportedly started after an air-conditioner compressor exploded inside the nursery, according to rescue officials.The blaze broke out at around 7 am in the gynaecology ward of the hospital on the third floor of the MCH ward, in Pakistan's federal capital. Rescue teams were deployed to the hospital and worked to extinguish the fire and evacuate those inside while carrying out cooling operations at the site.According to the district administration, 14 of the 15 children killed were completely burnt.The incident has raised concerns over safety measures in the hospital's neonatal and maternity facilities.Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered an immediate investigation into the incident and directed authorities to identify those responsible and take strict action. He expressed deep grief over the deaths, saying that a tragedy involving children was an “irreparable loss”, and said he shared the grief of the bereaved parents.The Prime Minister also directed authorities to conduct a detailed review of fire-safety arrangements and the factors that contributed to the incident, with the aim of preventing similar tragedies in hospitals.Meanwhile, an inquiry committee headed by the additional deputy commissioner general has also been formed to determine how the fire started and establish responsibility. The blaze broke out in the hospital’s gynaecology ward, where the nursery was located.
Article Summary: 15 newborns died after a fire broke out in the gynaecology ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad. The fire reportedly started after an air-conditioner compressor exploded inside the nursery, according to rescue sources. Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered an immediate investigation into the incident.

Article Title: Five labourers gunned down at construction site in Pakistan's Balochistan
Article Text: Five labourers from Pakistan’s Punjab province were shot dead at a construction site in Balochistan’s Pishin district, a provincial government official said Tuesday, according to news agency PTI.The labourers were killed by unidentified gunmen in Saranan town on Monday morning, Balochistan government spokesperson Shahid Rind said. Their bodies were sent to their hometowns in Punjab for burial.Arrangements were made to transport the bodies to their respective villages in Ahmedpur Sharqia and Bahawalpur, Rind said. Security forces have launched a search operation to track down the attackers.Balochistan chief minister Sarfaraz Bugti condemned the killings and vowed action against those responsible."Those shedding the blood of innocent laborers deserve no leniency," Bugti said in a statement issued by his office. "The cowardly acts of terrorists cannot weaken the provincial government's resolve."Saranan town has witnessed militant attacks since last week. A few days ago, gunmen attacked a police station in the town and fled with weapons, ammunition and two vehicles.Banned Baloch insurgent groups have frequently targeted workers and labourers from other provinces working in Balochistan.In July, five barbers from Multan were shot dead in Mashkail town after armed men on motorcycles opened fire at their barber shop.Last month, six labourers from Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa were abducted in the Nasirabad area of Turbat district. Their bullet-riddled bodies were later found in a remote area, police said.Security and law enforcement agencies have been conducting a large-scale operation against insurgent groups in parts of Balochistan since early July. However, the attacks have continued.In a separate incident on Sunday, five policemen were injured when two unidentified men hurled a hand grenade at a police post in Ambar tehsil of Mohmand district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.Police retaliated with gunfire, forcing the attackers to flee. The injured policemen were taken to a nearby hospital and are said to be out of danger. An investigation is underway.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which borders Afghanistan, has witnessed recurring militant violence, including attacks linked to insurgent groups, cross-border movement of fighters and repeated military operations.
Article Summary: The labourers were killed by unidentified gunmen in Saranan town on Monday morning. Security forces have launched a search operation to track down the attackers. Baloch insurgent groups have frequently targeted workers and labourers from other provinces working in Balochistan. In July, five barbers from Multan were shot dead in Mashkail town.

Article Title: Pakistan army officer pulls gun, fires in air amid student protest at Peshawar university- video
Article Text:
Sarhad University, Peshawar, Pakistan (Picture from X)

A Pakistan army officer opened fire into the air during a student protest at Sarhad University in Peshawar, triggering chaos and a scuffle on the campus, according to local media reports and videos circulating online.The incident comes amid growing unrest in Pakistan, with protests and demonstrations also being reported from Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and Balochistan, adding to the challenges facing the country's military and political establishment.According to reports, the officer, said to be a colonel, was the husband of a faculty member at Sarhad University. He reportedly got into a heated confrontation with protesting students, which soon escalated into a physical scuffle.Videos shared by several social media accounts purportedly show the officer striking students with a stick amid the confrontation. As tensions escalated, he allegedly pulled out a pistol and initially pointed it towards the protesters before raising the weapon in the air.The officer was then seen firing shots into the air, sparking panic and further uproar on the university campus.Reports said the officer has been taken into custody, while the Pakistan army has ordered an inquiry into the incident.
Article Summary: Pakistan army officer opened fire during student protest at Sarhad University. Incident triggered chaos and a scuffle on the campus, according to reports. Incident comes amid growing unrest in Pakistan, with protests and demonstrations also being reported from Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and Balochistan.

Article Title: ‘CTA intentionally prevented’: PTI alleges negligence over Imran Khan’s hospital visit
Article Text:
Imran Khan’s medical care under scrutiny

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think the inquiry committee established by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif will lead to accountability? Yes, it will No, it won't 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party of former Prime Minister Imran Khan, on Monday criticised what it called the “continued failure” of authorities at a state-run hospital, alleging that a CT Coronary Angiography (CTA) scheduled for Khan was not conducted despite cardiologists warning of potential cardiac complications.In a statement on Sunday, PTI central secretary Information Sheikh Waqas Akram said authorities had failed to provide the 73-year-old Khan with the medically recommended diagnostic test despite a functional CT scanner being available at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), Dawn reported."This cannot be dismissed as an isolated administrative lapse; it reflects a deeply troubling pattern,” Akram said.Akram also cited a Supreme Court order directing Khan to undergo a comprehensive medical examination and treatment at Shifa International Hospital.He alleged that authorities had bypassed the directive and instead transferred Khan to a facility where the CT angiography was not conducted.“When the necessary facilities were available at Shifa International, deliberately taking Khan to a hospital unable or unwilling to perform the procedure raises a grave question: was the decision made in advance to prevent the CT Coronary Angiography from being conducted?” he asked."Even the government’s own doctors considered this diagnostic test necessary,” Akram added.Akram said a government medical board examined Khan on August 10 after he complained of heart palpitations and severe headaches.He said a cardiologist at PIMS had recommended a CTA on August 1 after Khan experienced fluctuating blood pressure and restlessness, citing potential cardiac complications given his age and prolonged isolation.Taking note of the reports, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday formed an inquiry committee, headed by the Establishment Division secretary, to establish the facts and determine responsibility.Commenting on the Prime Minister’s decision to constitute an inquiry committee following reports that Imran Khan’s CTA was not conducted, Akram said the move raised “serious questions as to why the medically recommended test was not conducted in the first instance. Why coordination between the cardiology and radiology departments had failed, and why Imran Khan was not taken to Shifa International despite the availability of the required facilities there”."Imran Khan’s heart health cannot be subjected to political calculations, administrative excuses or further delay,” Akram said."Political victimisation must never be permitted to endanger a human life through the denial or postponement of essential medical care. The decision to take him to a facility where the required test was not conducted, despite the availability of the necessary facilities at Shifa International, has created serious concerns that the procedure was intentionally prevented,” he alleged."The government and all relevant authorities will bear full responsibility for any further deterioration in his condition,” Akram added.Meanwhile, former India captains Sunil Gavaskar, Kapil Dev and Dilip Vengsarkar are among 21 former international cricket captains who have written to Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, urging authorities to ensure proper medical treatment and the welfare of Imran Khan.The letter, initiated by former Australia captain Greg Chappell, marks the second appeal by former international cricketers calling for humane treatment and adequate medical care for the 73-year-old Khan.Khan was arrested on August 5, 2023, in connection with a corruption case and has remained in custody since then. He is currently lodged in Adiala Jail, a detention facility on the outskirts of Rawalpindi.Khan’s relatives and supporters have repeatedly alleged human rights violations and accused authorities of restricting his access to adequate medical care, family visits and legal counsel.
Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party of former Prime Minister Imran Khan, on Monday criticised what it called the “continued failure” of authorities at a state-run hospital. PTI alleges that a CT Coronary Angiography (CTA) scheduled for Khan was not conducted despite cardiologists warning of potential cardiac complications. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday formed an inquiry committee, headed by the Establishment Division secretary.

Article Title: ‘You are powerful, but remember 1971?’ Pakistani politician takes fresh swipe at Army
Article Text:
Fazlur Rehman (File photo)

(With ANI inputs)

Pakistani politician and Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam (F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman continued his verbal attacks on the Pakistan Army, recalling the military's decisive defeat in the 1971 war with India that led to the creation of Bangladesh, then known as East Pakistan.“‘We are the protectors of this country. No one’s father can harm this country.’ I agree, you are very powerful,” Rehman remarked at a JUI (F) convention in Peshawar, targeting Pakistan’s top military leadership.He recalled how the Pakistan Army laid down its arms in 1971, just a day after then-President and military ruler General Yahya Khan declared that it would fight until the end."But I remember, and maybe there are some elders who remember, that in December 1971, one day before laying down arms, General Yahya Khan addressed the army and said, we will fight in the streets, in the deserts, in the fields, in the factories, in the mountains, and we will fight against them. We will fight. We heard these big words then," Rehman added.The JUI-F further chief questioned why the public is being subjected to "severe hardships" while the establishment remains "insensitive" to their misery.“Why are you putting the country and the people to the test? Why are you having fun when your public is suffering? And today is 2026. When the revolution came in Afghanistan in 1989, and the war started, now you tell me, it’s been 45-46 years, blood has been flowing on the same line for about half a century.When blood flows like this, then it is a sign of geographical changes,” Rehman remarked.Warning that persistent state oppression and ongoing conflict threaten the nation’s integrity and could signal territorial disintegration, he stated, “It is a sign of oppression. Then at least inform us of your intentions. We are tolerating it and will continue to tolerate it. It will continue. A few more days, my dear, just a few more days. We are forced to take a breath in the shade of oppression. If we endure the oppression for a little longer, if we suffer, if we cry, it is the legacy of our ancestors. We are helpless.”Rehman’s remarks came days after he challenged the military to enter politics directly, declaring, “If you want to do politics, then take off the uniform and come; participate in the elections, and it will become clear what votes people give to those in uniform. It is your prerogative to give government to whomever you want, and to snatch it away from whomever you wish.”
Article Summary: Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam (F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman continued his verbal attacks on the Pakistan Army. He recalled the military's decisive defeat in the 1971 war with India that led to the creation of Bangladesh. He questioned why the public is being subjected to "severe hardships" while the establishment remains "insensitive"

Article Title: Pakistan: Security official killed by unidentified gunmen; 5 cops injured in separate grenade blast
Article Text:
According to police, two unidentified armed men targeted the security official. (Photo credit: IANS)

Five policemen injured in grenade attack

A security official was killed on Sunday after unidentified gunmen opened fire in northwest Pakistan, police said, according to news agency PTI.The incident took place within the jurisdiction of Badaber Police Station on the outskirts of Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.According to police, two unidentified armed men riding a motorcycle targeted the official, who was posted with the Counter Terrorism Department.He was killed on the spot, while the assailants fled the scene following the attack. Police cordoned off the area and launched a search operation to trace the attackers.No individual or group has so far claimed responsibility for the attack.In a separate incident in Mohmand district, five policemen were injured when two unidentified men hurled a hand grenade at a police post in Ambar tehsil, police said.Police retaliated with gunfire, forcing the attackers to flee. The injured policemen were taken to a nearby hospital and are said to be out of danger. An investigation is underway.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which borders Afghanistan, has witnessed recurring militant violence, cross-border movement of fighters and military operations.Pakistan's federal government has blamed the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) for attacks in areas bordering Afghanistan since a ceasefire agreement between the two sides ended in November 2022.
Article Summary: A security official was killed on Sunday after unidentified gunmen opened fire in northwest Pakistan. In a separate incident, five policemen were injured when two unidentified men hurled a hand grenade at a police post in Ambar tehsil. The injured policemen were taken to a nearby hospital and are said to be out of danger.

Article Title: Pakistan power crisis: Karachi residents riot amid outages lasting hours, block major roads
Article Text:
Protesters blocked major roads and intersections, burned tyres and clashed with K-Electric personnel over prolonged blackouts (ANI photo)

Power protests erupted across several parts of Karachi as residents took to the streets over prolonged and unannounced outages, blocking major roads and burning tyres while demanding restoration of electricity.Demonstrations were reported in Pak Colony, Liaquatabad, Gharibabad, Nishtar Road, Bhimpura and Ranchore Line, disrupting traffic across key parts of Pakistan’s commercial capital. In Liaquatabad, protesters blocked major intersections, while clashes between traders and K-Electric (KE) staff over outages escalated into tyre-burning on Nishtar Road, as reported by local news outle Dawn.Residents said they were facing 12 hours or more of daily power cuts, often without adequate notice. The outages have also disrupted water supplies as pumping stations remain shut when electricity is unavailable, adding to public anger.“Bill-paying citizens are being punished with 12-hour load-shedding,” a protester in Liaquatabad said.The crisis also hit businesses and households, with residents reporting spoiled food, disrupted studies and sleepless nights as fans remained unusable during blackouts.The protests compounded an already severe traffic situation in the city. Roads were also closed for traditional Chup Tazia processions, while the power protests triggered additional blockades. Traffic police diverted vehicles to alternative routes, but those too became congested.Asif Khan, a private-sector employee, told Dawn he took four hours to travel from SITE to Liaquatabad after leaving work around 5pm. Another commuter said an ambulance carrying his feverish mother was stuck for about two hours near Civic Centre while they were travelling to a doctor in Saddar.“We pay bills on time but still face 12-hour power outages. Today we couldn’t even reach home,” commuter Imran from Gharibabad said.KE, however, attributed the prolonged outages in some affected areas to electricity theft and unpaid bills. A company spokesperson said outstanding dues from defaulters in Bandhani Colony and Rexer Line had crossed PKR 3 billion, adding that the duration of load-shedding depended on “electricity theft and the level of losses in the area”.The protests come as Karachi continues to grapple with an electricity crisis that is also affecting water supply, businesses and daily life across densely populated neighbourhoods.
Article Summary: Demonstrations reported in Pak Colony, Liaquatabad, Gharibabad, Nishtar Road, Bhimpura and Ranchore Line. Protesters blocked major roads and intersections, burned tyres and clashed with K-Electric personnel. Residents said they were facing 12 hours or more of daily power cuts, often without adequate notice.

Article Title: 'India could use water as weapon': Pakistan minister as Indus Waters Treaty remains in abeyance
Article Text:
Pakistan minister Ahsan Iqbal (File photo)

Pakistan minister Ahsan Iqbal has said India could “weaponise” the Indus Water Treaty (IWT) and expressed hope that “better sense” would prevail to prevent the two neighbours from going to war again, this time over water.He noted that the treaty had remained “untouchable” for almost seven decades since it was signed in 1960, but New Delhi has now been kept in abeyance “unilaterally."“...Indus Water Treaty that has stood the test of time for the last 70 years. India and Pakistan fought several wars, but it (IWT) was considered untouchable because it is an international agreement, and this time around the Indian government has unilaterally held it in abeyance... first time probably water has been weaponised in history,” Iqbal told the Asia Society.“We (Pakistan) now face this threat that they (India) can use water as a weapon to deny Pakistan when it needs it for its crops and release it when we don't need it... We are using all the diplomatic means to make sure that we don't have future wars on water because we have already seen lots of wars,” the minister added.He further stated that South Asian countries should instead focus on issues such as development, poverty, illiteracy and the youth “bulge”, describing the region as the “least integrated” in the world."So we hope that there is better sense in our neighbour's (India) mind and we don't see that water is weaponised and we go to another conflict with India over water because Pakistan cannot surrender at any cost the future of its 250 million people for its food security and right of water. If we let it happen, then every state that is on the lower side of water supply would be hostage to any country that controls the rivers," the Pakistan Muslim League (Nawaz) leader remarked.Iqbal's remarks came days after Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif warned India of a “direct response” for putting the IWT in abeyance.“India proved itself an enemy of peace by unilaterally and illegally suspending the Indus Waters Treaty. I declare in clear terms that every single drop of Pakistan's water is our red line. If India does not come to its senses, it will be responded to directly,” Sharif said on August 13, on the eve of Pakistan's Independence Day.New Delhi put the agreement in abeyance following the Pahalgam terror attack in April last year. Since then, Pakistani leaders have repeatedly called water their “red line” and threatened India over the move, describing it as an “act of war.”
Article Summary: Ahsan Iqbal says India could use water as a weapon to deny Pakistan when it needs it for its crops. New Delhi put the agreement in abeyance following the Pahalgam terror attack in April last year. Pakistani leaders have repeatedly called water their “red line” and threatened India.

Article Title: ‘In contempt for gathering people’: Pak blames ex PM Imran Khan’s party for hospital transfer
Article Text:
Pakistan government statement on Imran Khan's hospital transfer

Poll Vote & Share your view How do you view the involvement of PTI workers during Imran Khan transfer to the hospital? Justified, they were supporting their leader Unsure 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Govt says court order was followed

NEW DELHI: The Pakistan government on Saturday blamed jailed former prime minister Imran Khan ’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party for his transfer to a state-run hospital instead of the private facility ordered by the Supreme Court for his medical checkup.Information minister Attaullah Tarar said the government was forced to take 73-year-old Khan to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) after a large number of PTI workers gathered outside Shifa International Hospital.The development came after Khan’s sister, Uzma Khan, approached the Supreme Court alleging that the government and senior officials had violated its order to shift the former prime minister to the private hospital.The Supreme Court had on August 18 directed authorities to transfer Khan from Adiala jail to Shifa Hospital within two days and keep him there until the next hearing on September 16. Instead, Khan was taken to PIMS and later returned to jail after doctors declared him fit.Tarar alleged that PTI workers gathered along the route to Shifa Hospital, removed barriers and created social media content, leaving authorities with no option but to shift Khan elsewhere.“Contempt has definitely happened,” Tarar said, accusing Khan’s sister and PTI of violating the court’s directions by turning the medical checkup into a political issue.The minister maintained that the government had implemented the Supreme Court’s order “in letter and spirit”. He said the medical examination was conducted transparently, Khan’s sister was present and doctors from Shifa Hospital were involved in the process.The Supreme Court’s order followed months of concerns raised by Khan’s family and supporters over his health, particularly an eye condition diagnosed earlier this year. Khan was taken to PIMS several times after being diagnosed with right central retinal vein occlusion in late January.A report submitted by jail authorities to the Supreme Court said his eye condition had improved significantly and that his vision was “almost normal”.Khan has been lodged in Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail since 2023 in connection with several cases.
Article Summary: Pakistan government blames jailed former prime minister Imran Khan ’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party for his transfer to a state-run hospital. Information minister Attaullah Tarar said the government was forced to take 73-year-old Khan to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences. Tarar alleged that PTI workers gathered along the route to Shifa Hospital, removed barriers and created social media content.

Article Title: Big crisis brewing in Rawalpindi? Pakistan deploys army for ‘sensitive duties’
Article Text:
The decision comes days after a man allegedly linked to former prime minister Imran Khan's party.

Army deployment follows security incident

Rawalpindi has strategic importance

The Pakistan government has authorised the deployment of the army in Rawalpindi for six months following a request from the Punjab home department for what it described as "sensitive security duties".The decision allows three companies of the Pakistan Army to be deployed in the city under Article 245 of the Pakistani Constitution, which permits the armed forces to assist the civil administration in maintaining security."The federal government, exercising the powers conferred under Article 245 of the Constitution of Pakistan, is pleased to authorise the deployment of three companies of the Pakistan Army for sensitive security duties in Rawalpindi," according to a notification issued by the Ministry of Interior and Narcotics Control on Friday.The notification said the deployment was intended to prevent a potential security problem and ensure that authorities could respond quickly if an unexpected situation arose.It said that the decision was taken "to avoid any undesirable situation as well as to respond effectively in any unforeseen situation as per the requirement of the district administration".The decision comes days after a man allegedly linked to former prime minister Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party opened fire at security forces in Rawalpindi.He was subsequently killed in retaliatory firing.State-run PTV News, citing security sources, reported that the attacker was a resident of Khyber district and an "active PTI member". According to the report, a PTI flag, bullets and weapons were recovered from him.The PTI, however, rejected any connection with the incident. The party said it had nothing to do with terrorism and accused authorities of attempting to associate the party with the attack.The deployment is particularly significant because Rawalpindi is home to the Pakistan Army's General Headquarters, the military's top command centre.The city is therefore an important military and administrative centre, and the decision to deploy army personnel there comes amid heightened security concerns following the recent shooting incident.The deployment has been authorised for six months, with the troops to perform duties requested by the district administration under the constitutional provision allowing the military to assist civilian authorities.
Article Summary: Three companies of the Pakistan Army will be deployed in Rawalpindi for six months. The decision comes after a man allegedly linked to Imran Khan's party opened fire in the city. The deployment is intended to prevent a potential security problem and ensure that authorities can respond quickly.

Article Title: ‘The flood is on its way’: How 400 Nepal students escaped in time
Article Text:
A school bag is full of mud brought in by the recent flash floods, at the Shree Bagheswori Madhyamik School in Nepal. (Photo: AP)

Principal orders students to higher ground

Bags remain on desks after evacuation

17,000 children need humanitarian aid

Morning assembly was about to begin at Bageshwori Higher Secondary School on August 26 when teachers learned that floodwaters were heading towards Baireni.Principal Prakash Malla told students to move to higher ground. Around 400 children were out of the school before the water arrived.Binita Ramtel had barely settled into her classroom and put down her bag when students were told to leave. "I had just arrived at the school, I had just kept my bag in the classroom and was preparing to come to the ground for the morning assembly, then the teachers made the announcement that the flood was on its way and asked us to evacuate, after which we fled from here," Binita told ANI while visiting her classroom.It was after 9am local time when the water entered Baireni. Students would normally have been arriving then for an assembly lasting about 15-20 minutes. Bageshwori Higher Secondary School stands close to the river.A guardian living upstream had alerted the school about the approaching flood. Science teacher Dipendra Wagle said one of the staff members received information from Nuwakot as students were getting ready for physical training (PT) or assembly."When the students were preparing to attend the PT or the assembly, one of our teachers got information about the flood from Nuwakot. After that, our teacher Prakash Malla (Principal) announced from the office to get out of the school and all students ran away from here and are safe," he told ANI.Another warning about the water moving downstream reached Rajkumar Rimal through his spouse. Rimal, whose child attended the school, was working in a field at the time. His spouse told him that flooding had already hit the Betrawati River in Nuwakot.Speaking with ANI he said: "I was working in the field that day, and my spouse called me, warning that the Betrawati in Nuwakot had already been swept away by the flood and it is running downstream. The status of the students in school was my primary concern, as the two schools here are of direct concern and threat of the flood. I hurriedly came to the school and saw everyone was panicking and teachers were shifting the students to the safer grounds from here; I also helped them to evacuate students to the higher grounds successfully. " He later joined the evacuation at the school.When Binita returned almost a week later, the playground was covered in sand and her classroom in sludge and debris.The sudden departure was evident in what students had left behind. Bags remained on desks. Binita and her friend Prasamsha Magrati came across other students' damp belongings, along with tiffin boxes containing uneaten food.Marks left on the walls indicated both the level reached by the floodwater and the damage inside the school.Baireni lies on the Prithvi Highway. Flooding inundated the town on Wednesday, leaving deposits of mud and sand that reached as much as two metres above the river's level.Mud and sludge remained across the school premises almost a week later, while debris continued to give off a foul smell.Binita also lost belongings she used at school. "If it is provided by the local cooperatives; if not, then I am alive, I will buy it again," she said.Around 17,000 children required humanitarian assistance after the August 26 floods, according to UNICEF estimates. The reported toll had crossed 900, with hundreds of people still missing.UNICEF appealed for USD 17.2 million to keep the emergency response going and support the initial recovery effort as assessments of overall needs continued.Relief teams and search operations remained active in the heavily affected districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading. For Bageshwori Higher Secondary School, there was still no clear date for classes to resume.
Article Summary: Baireni lies on the Prithvi Highway. Flooding inundated the town on Wednesday, leaving deposits of mud and sand that reached as much as two metres above the river's level. UNICEF appealed for USD 17.2 million to keep the emergency response going.

Article Title: Teams, equipped with searchlights and drones, walk through mud, silt to search for survivors in tunnels
Article Text:
File photo: Nepal Army rescue team navigate through the dark, waterlogged tunnel of the Rasuwa Hydropower Project, in Rasuwa district, Nepal.

TOI

TRISHULI BAZAAR/DEHRADUN: At least 955 people were dead and 4,471 missing across Nepal and Tibet by Monday evening as rescue teams pushed deeper into mud- and water-filled hydropower tunnels in Rasuwa and Nuwakot and searches continued across the border in Gyirong.The break-up comprised 939 dead and 3,925 missing in Nepal, as per National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority’s latest update at 6pm Monday, and 16 dead and 546 missing in Tibet in the latest official Chinese tally.Of Nepal’s 3,925 missing, 592 were foreign nationals and 639 were linked to hydropower projects. The overall missing figure had been revised down from 4,247, while the hydropower-linked count fell sharply from 933 as attendance, rescue and missing-person lists were reconciled. NDRRMA said 11,379 people had been rescued.Joint teams led by Nepal army continued search and rescue operations inside hydropower project tunnels, recovering three more bodies from two tunnels while returning from another after finding no sign of life or bodies inside.Nepal army spokesperson Brig Gen Rajaram Basnet toldthat a rescue team entered Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project tunnel, where 14 people had been feared trapped.“The team, equipped with searchlights and drones, reached the end of the 250m-deep tunnel. However, they failed to find any trace of any person after much effort and finally returned,” Basnet said.At Chilime Hydropower Project, another joint team comprising foreign experts entered around 100m before encountering a section completely buried under mud and silt.One of the most difficult operations remained at Trishuli-3A, where teams carried out a controlled blast at around 2am Monday, Nepal time, to create an entry portal after struggling to breach the buried tunnel. “Additionally, two excavators have also been deployed at a depth of around 10m to create an opening and clear water, mud and silt from within the tunnel. Search and rescue operations are also going on at the Trishuli-3B site,” Basnet said.The latest official update said teams at Trishuli-3A had located the tunnel head and were supplying air through a co­mpressor while draining operations continued, and an alternative route at the rear had been cleared for around 15m. At Upper Trishuli-1, rescuers had searched up to around 300m into the Hakku tunnel and 200m at Mailung, while specialist teams and excavators remained deployed at Trishuli-3B.Basnet said Nepal army alone had rescued 3,596 people, including 338 foreigners, by Monday afternoon.Across the border in Tibet, rescue crews continued trying to restore ground access to devastated Gyirong port. By noon Monday, heavy machinery had reopened G216 highway to within around 1.1km of the port, narrowing the final road gap to the core disaster zone.
Article Summary: At least 955 people dead and 4,471 missing across Nepal and Tibet. Rescue teams pushed deeper into mud- and water-filled hydropower tunnels in Rasuwa and Nuwakot and searches continued across the border in Gyirong.

Article Title: Nepal toll 955; 4471 missing even as tunnel searchers push deeper
Article Text:
File photo: A rescuer works at the entrance of a tunnel at Chilime Hydropower Plant as rescue operations continue for people trapped inside.

At least 955 people were dead in flash floods and 4,471 missing across Nepal and Tibet by Monday evening — 639 of Nepal’s 3,925 missing people being linked to hydropower projects.Nepal Army spokesperson Brig Gen Rajaram Basnet told TOI a rescue team entered Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project tunnel, where 14 people had been feared trapped. “The team, equipped with searchlights and drones, reached the end of the 250m-deep tunnel. However, they failed to find any trace of any person after much effort and finally returned.”At Chilime hydel, another joint team comprising foreign experts entered around 100m before encountering a section buried under mud and silt. One of the most difficult operations was at Trishuli-3A, where a controlled blast was carried out to create an entry portal.With roads and bridges washed out, drone pilots are flying over debris, using thermal cameras to look for stranded people and bodies, and carrying relief material. Nepalese living abroad and global mapping volunteers, meanwhile, are pitching in by scanning satellite imagery to help map the flood zone.
Article Summary: At least 955 people were dead in flash floods and 4,471 missing across Nepal and Tibet by Monday evening. 639 of Nepal’s 3,925 missing people being linked to hydropower projects. Rescue team entered Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project tunnel, where 14 people had been feared trapped.

Article Title: Nepal floods: Bank vaults full of cash washed away; police struggle to secure them
Article Text:
Som​e of these vaults contain huge amounts of cash and other valuables.

DEHRADUN: Apart from searching for hundreds of people missing in the flash floods, Nepal’s police are facing another daunting task of tracing and securing missing vaults of at least 20 banks washed away in the deluge and preventing them from falling into the wrong hands. Some of these vaults contain huge amounts of cash and other valuables, officials told TOI Monday.DIG Abi Narayan Kafle said that amid the challenging post-flood situation, the force’s first priority is to look for those missing, but at the same time they need to maintain law and order in the affected areas.“There were banks in Rasuwa, Dhading, Chitwan, and other places that were significantly damaged. Many of their vaults containing cash and other valuable items such as gold were either washed away or got buried under heavy silt. Our personnel are now putting all their efforts to find and secure those vaults. There have been incidents where people broke open the washed-away vaults and stole cash.”The development came after police in Dhading district arrested 29 people for allegedly stealing NPR 92 lakh from a washed-away vault from the Upper Rasuwa area. “On Sunday evening, our personnel managed to secure a vault of the Agricultural Development Bank’s Dhunge branch in Trishuli.The task took them nearly eight hours,” Kafle said.He added the vault had NPR 1.5 crore cash and other valuables, including gold worth NPR 50 crore. In another instance, police secured a vault of ‘Krishi Vikas Bank’, Nuwakot.The police spokesperson further said the force has deployed 7,894 personnel in the ongoing rescue operations.
Article Summary: Nepal’s police are facing another daunting task of tracing and securing missing vaults of at least 20 banks washed away in the deluge. Some of these vaults contain huge amounts of cash and other valuables, officials told TOI.

Article Title: Nepal floods: Avalanche from 5,200 metres raced down Himalayas at 167 kmph, triggering deadly deluge
Article Text:
Nepal-China border disaster has killed over 900 people and left thousands missing.

The ice-rock avalanche that triggered Nepal's devastating August 26 floods moved with extraordinary speed, covering around 22 kilometres to Rasuwagadhi in just over seven minutes, according to a preliminary study by Nepalese scientists.The mass travelled at an estimated average speed of 46.3 metres per second, or about 167 kmph, as it plunged from the high Himalayas into the river system below, news agency PTI reported.The study, commissioned by the Nepal Environment Society (NES), found that the massive mass of ice, rock and debris began falling from the northern part of the Langtang–Lirung area of Rasuwa at around 8.37 am.Starting at an altitude of approximately 5,200 metres, the avalanche descended steep terrain before reaching the Lhende River at about 2,930 metres. It then surged downstream through the Bhotekoshi and into the Trishuli river system, generating a powerful debris-laden flood.The speed of the initial surge helps explain the devastation downstream. Although the flow slowed to around 73 kmph between Rasuwagadhi and Betrabati, it continued carrying enormous quantities of rock, sediment and soil. Farther downstream, its speed fell to around 22 kmph, but the debris-loaded torrent retained enough force to cause widespread destruction.Satellite imagery showed major geographical changes across an area of about 10 square kilometres, while a section of glacier covering approximately 0.56 square kilometres had broken away.The findings also challenge the initial assumption that the disaster was caused by a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF). Researchers found no evidence of a GLOF after analysing satellite imagery, hydrological and meteorological data, terrain characteristics and changes in elevation and slope along the river system.There was also no evidence of exceptionally heavy rainfall in the upper watershed on the day of the disaster, weakening the theory that an extreme cloudburst or rainfall event alone caused the floods.The study noted another striking feature: water levels and river flow in the Rasuwagadhi and Syafrubesi areas fell several hours before the destructive surge arrived. At Rasuwagadhi, the average water level declined between 5 am and 8 am, while flow at Syafrubesi began falling at around 7 am.Scientists, however, said further field investigation is needed to establish the precise geological mechanism, the contribution of melting ice and whether the river was temporarily blocked upstream.The avalanche also caused extensive damage to Nepal’s hydropower infrastructure. Preliminary Nepal Electricity Authority data cited in the study showed that 13 hydropower projects and one solar project were affected, taking around 431 MW of generation capacity out of the system.The floods killed at least 900 people, according to authorities, with thousands still missing. Rescue teams were continuing to search for hundreds of workers believed to be trapped inside hydropower tunnels in the worst-hit districts of Rasuwa and Nuwakot.The disaster has also left behind the threat of further landslides, unstable glaciers and potentially dangerous lakes, raising concerns that the Himalayan region could face additional flooding even after the initial torrent has passed.
Article Summary: The mass travelled at an estimated average speed of 46.3 metres per second, or about 167 kmph, as it plunged from the high Himalayas into the river system below. The study, commissioned by the Nepal Environment Society, found that the massive mass of ice, rock and debris began falling from the northern part of the Langtang–Lirung area of Rasuwa at around 8.37 am.
